Purpose
Prepare a controlled test design for Priya’s review—not a launch. The test evaluates whether clearer pricing-page paths reduce avoidable unsupported-condition routing while preserving existing controls.

Design
- Channel: organic only; no paid traffic.
- Allocation: pricing-page sessions split 50/50 between control and treatment.
- Control: existing pricing-page paths.
- Treatment: separate entry points for the bounded under-50, simple-deployment Helio Start path and the assisted path.
- Test window: October 20–November 16, 2025.

Invariants
All existing eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, and support-routing rules remain unchanged. No unrelated pricing-page layout or UI change is allowed during the test.

Decision criteria
- Primary success threshold: at least a 25% relative reduction in Helio Start eligibility-flow starts that later route out for an existing unsupported condition.
- Guardrail: eligible-workspace admission completion declines by no more than 1.5 percentage points.
- Guardrail: account-level support time at P90 increases by no more than 10 minutes.

Readout and constraints
Owen will read three complete weekly cohorts plus the November 10–16 stabilization cohort. No paid traffic, pipeline target, forecast credit, or unrelated pricing-page change is permitted. Priya approval: pending. Result-decision date: pending.

input.body:
Q4 PRICING PATH CLARITY TEST — OUTCOME MEMO
January 1, 2028

Decision
The certified test passed the predeclared path-quality threshold and both guardrails. It supports the tested path-separated design as the default experience for organic pricing-page traffic. The treatment was rolled out to 100% of organic traffic on November 26, 2025, and the control was retired.

Certified result
- Scope: 3,286 organic pricing-page sessions; 1,639 control and 1,647 treatment, tested October 20–November 16, 2025.
- Path-quality threshold: PASSED. Unsupported-condition route-outs fell from 38/344 control starts (11.0%) to 25/352 treatment starts (7.1%), a 35.7% relative reduction versus the predeclared minimum of 25%.
- Admission-completion guardrail: PASSED. Eligible-workspace admission completion was 43.8% control versus 44.1% treatment; there was no decline, versus the allowed maximum decline of 1.5 percentage points.
- Support-time guardrail: PASSED. Account-level support time at P90 was 71 minutes control versus 74 minutes treatment, a 3-minute increase versus the allowed maximum of 10 minutes.
- The favorable direction held across all three weekly cohorts and the November 10–16 stabilization cohort. No unrelated pricing-page layout or UI change occurred.

Rollout supported
The result supports using separate bounded entry paths for the under-50, simple-deployment Helio Start path and assisted needs as the default organic pricing-page experience. It supports a narrower path-quality conclusion: fewer unsupported self-serve starts with admission completion and P90 support time within the predeclared limits.

Boundaries unchanged
The result and rollout do not change eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, or support-routing rules. Customer Success assisted routes remain in place; no new lifecycle branch was introduced. The evidence is limited to organic pricing-page traffic. Paid acquisition, unrelated pricing-page changes, pipeline targets, and forecast credit remain outside scope.

Commercial conclusions not established
This test does not establish revenue lift, pricing-driven revenue or conversion attribution, incremental acquisition, paid-acquisition economics, pipeline impact, forecastable performance, or forecast credit. It does not establish downstream customer value, retention, scale readiness, or a general commercial effect beyond the measured path-quality outcome. Reliable rollout and favorable funnel-quality evidence are not, by themselves, evidence of financial impact.

Archive date: 2028-01-01
Audience: Onboarding and retrospective use

Purpose
This note records the shape of the original Helio Start effort so that later teams do not confuse the initial sub-50-seat motion with a blanket small-customer entitlement or a low-price plan.

Duration and arc
The original effort ran from mid-June 2023 through the August 11, 2023 controlled-beta/live-path transition — roughly two months. The work began as Q3 scenario work under the Helio Start name, moved through a June 29 guardrail decision and July discovery-candidate intake, then concentrated on late-July instrumentation readiness and the August bounded-path gate. By August 11, the path was described as live for teams under 50 seats, while the same period still included a narrow invited-account controlled beta; the practical lesson is that “live” referred to a constrained path, not unrestricted admission.

Core workstreams
- Positioning and segment definition: establish Helio Start as the sub-50-seat motion, while explicitly avoiding “cheap plan” framing and avoiding a launch promise before the operating gates cleared.
- Eligibility and candidate intake: move beyond seat count and ARR. Candidates needed to be eligible for the intended path; those fields alone were not sufficient for acceptance.
- Product and engineering readiness: define the supported, simple-deployment shape, confirm connector access, and identify cases that would require work outside the product’s bounded path.
- Instrumentation and measurement: build and validate the event/readout foundation for workspace creation, eligibility, activation, assisted setup, unsupported routing, and support load before scaling the motion.
- Lifecycle and onboarding: provide a safe self-serve education path after workspace creation, including the setup checklist and first-integration guidance, with copy that qualified the guidance by eligibility and fit.
- Customer Success and support operations: make assisted setup and support workload visible, set support boundaries, and ensure unsupported or high-effort cases could be routed rather than silently admitted.
- Commercial governance: connect the offer to explicit guardrails, monitoring, evidence requirements, and stop rules rather than treating pricing-page demand as proof of product or operating-model readiness.

How the guardrails were meant to relate
Commercial guardrails were a control layer around a product- and eligibility-constrained experiment; they were not a substitute for either one.

1. Commercial eligibility was not “under 50 seats, therefore eligible.” Seat count defined the target segment, but seat count and ARR alone could not establish fit or readiness. Acceptance depended on the eligibility evidence and the completeness of the required baseline readout.
2. Product constraints came first. The intended path was for workspaces with a straightforward setup and supported connector access. Self-serve was not the right promise for accounts needing migration/import help, manual billing help, or other unsupported work. Those cases needed an assisted or out-of-path route, with the outcome captured in instrumentation.
3. Guardrails protected the bounded operating model. The decision framework paired a success measure with support-load and unsupported-admission guardrails, monitoring, and explicit stop rules. A commercial test could proceed only when the eligibility logic, product boundary, instrumentation, lifecycle experience, and support capacity were all sufficiently defined and evidenced.
4. Messaging had to preserve those dependencies. “Under 50” was a segment signal, not unconditional approval; “start” described a path available when the workspace was eligible and the guided setup fit its needs. Helio Start was not shorthand for a cheap plan, and commercial access could not override product limitations.

Retrospective takeaway
The durable design principle was: qualify the workspace first, admit only into a supported product path, instrument the full funnel and the exits, and use commercial guardrails to limit exposure while evidence is gathered. If any of those layers was missing, the right response was to narrow, assist, defer, or stop — not to broaden eligibility by changing the copy.

Timeline anchors
- 2023-06-14: Helio Start adopted as the working label for Q3 scenario work; not a launch promise and not a synonym for a cheap plan.
- 2023-06-29: guardrail decision landed.
- 2023-07-05: discovery-candidate intake created.
- 2023-07-13: seat count and ARR explicitly rejected as sufficient eligibility criteria.
- 2023-07-25: late-July instrumentation-readiness framing chosen over assuming an August beta.
- 2023-08-04 to 2023-08-09: bounded-path decision and controlled-beta readiness work, with the final guardrail check spanning eligibility, instrumentation, lifecycle, and support load.
- 2023-08-11: constrained path described as live for teams under 50 seats, alongside the narrow controlled-beta context.

Record status
Retrospective archive note. Later Helio Start pricing, lifecycle, and measurement work may use different definitions or operating limits; do not silently project those later rules backward onto this original effort.

arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft

Working draft for Priya’s 2027 year-end self-review window. First draft requested by November 19, 2027.

Operating-model decisions and claim discipline

I personally owned two things this year. First, I set the bounded operating frame for the November Helio Start paid batch: paid traffic stayed gated until the required paid-source trace, rollback control, staffed Customer Success coverage, and approved traffic conditions were confirmed. Priya approved the bounded batch, and Daniela authorized the November 1 launch once the operating gates were met. I maintained the approval boundary and treated the launch as live operational work, not as evidence of a mature acquisition outcome.

Second, I set the four-lane claim limits for the work. My lane was the operating decision and the explicit boundary around what could be claimed. Owen owned measurement, denominators, reporting semantics, source completeness, and exception reporting. Ines owned lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, and message-state work. Daniela owned source reliability, engineering release, rollback control, and reliability authority. I kept those lanes distinct rather than blending their evidence into a single project claim. Their contributions are material: Owen made the operating read measurable and auditable; Ines kept lifecycle and message-state decisions governed; and Daniela made the live enablement and rollback boundary reliable.

The four lanes also defined what I deliberately kept out of the self-review claims: pipeline and forecast treatment; early mature claims for the live cohort; and automatic expansion beyond the fifth consumer. I did not convert a small live-batch read into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale, and I did not treat the fifth-consumer reminder as a reason to expand the shared-state model automatically. December development outcomes also remain open; October and November evidence is progress, not completion of the required October–December cycle.

For the November paid batch, I made the operating decision and maintained the approval boundary; I did not claim ownership of the supporting measurement, lifecycle-state certification, source reliability, release, or rollback work. That separation is an operating-model result in itself: each decision was supported by the appropriate owner evidence rather than by a blended claim.

I also helped establish the incomplete-setup reminder as Lifecycle Systems’ fifth production consumer, not a sixth consumer. The operating model required a fresh evaluation for every possible display, with current setup, qualifying-human-admin status, active Customer Success work, and required state determining display, suppression, or hold. A held record was not treated as a queued delivery. These choices kept the reminder within the existing shared-state model and preserved the existing owner lanes. I did not authorize automatic expansion beyond that fifth consumer.

Evidence and bounded outcomes

I have been deliberate about distinguishing what was decided, what was observed, and what remains unproven. The November 1–7 reminder operation had 12,480 fresh evaluations. Of those, 1,615 displayed, 520 were suppressed because current Customer Success work was active, 186 were held because required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting, and 10,159 did not display because current setup or qualifying-human-admin conditions were not met. These are operating counts, not claims of customer impact, durable behavior change, or mature performance.

The paid-batch evidence is similarly bounded. By Owen’s November 5 operating snapshot, 12 paid-source eligibility-flow starts had reached final states: five admitted, four assisted, and three ineligible, with $1,580 in spend. Paid-source attribution reconciled through every final route, and no unsupported applicant entered the admitted path. This is a live operational-status read, not a mature-outcome read for the live cohort. The formal support-pause monitor had not begun because the admission count was still below its threshold. I will continue to avoid converting early routing and control evidence into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale.

The evidence boundary also requires acknowledging what did not occur during the November 1–7 reminder interval: no reusable audience was created, no failed rollback occurred, no incident stop was triggered, and no customer correction was recorded. Those facts demonstrate the bounded state of the operation; they do not prove that the system is broadly mature or that future intervals will behave the same way.

Team development

My leadership goal has been to make ownership legible and to develop independent operating judgment without absorbing other people’s lanes. Owen’s measurement and exception-reporting work includes definitions, denominators, bounded operating snapshots, source-completeness checks, and exception synthesis. Ines’s work includes lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, lifecycle-risk explanation, and message-state transitions and controls. Daniela’s work includes source-integrity and reliability checks, production enablement, engineering release control, and rollback readiness.

The Q4 development focuses for Owen and Ines remain open through the required December cycle. October and November submissions are evidence of progress, not completion of the October–December focus. Owen’s November operating read and Ines’s November lifecycle-risk explanation should be credited to their respective lanes, while each focus remains open until the required December cycle is completed and reviewed. I am preserving that status rather than prematurely marking either development focus complete. Daniela’s engineering authority likewise remains intact rather than being treated as a substitute for my operating decisions.

System reliability

The reliability improvement I helped drive was procedural as much as technical: explicit gates, fresh state evaluation, held-versus-queued semantics, active-work suppression, staffed backup handling, and a clear stop/correction boundary. The November paid batch launched only after the control evidence was available. Daniela verified the live enable and rollback controls and retained engineering authority. Ines maintained the lifecycle and message-state boundary. Owen provided the bounded measurement and exception read. The reminder operation’s agreed reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes show that the five-consumer operation remained coherent during the observed interval.

I do not interpret the absence of a failed rollback, incident stop, or customer correction as proof that reliability work is finished. The right claim is narrower: the controls were exercised in a bounded live interval without those recorded events, and the owner lanes and escalation boundaries held. Continued operation and the required December cycle are still needed before making broader claims.

Next-cycle focus

In the next cycle, I will continue to make explicit, reversible operating decisions with approval gates and evidence boundaries visible in the working record. I want to improve the handoff from live operating status to a genuinely mature outcome read: clear thresholds, complete observation windows, denominator discipline, and an explicit decision about when evidence is sufficient for expansion, continuation, or pause.

I will keep the five-consumer reminder operation within its current shared-state contract while reviewing held, suppressed, and displayed paths for operational clarity rather than optimizing display volume. I will also preserve the distinction between my decision lane and the owner lanes: Owen’s measurement and exception synthesis, Ines’s lifecycle governance and message-state work, and Daniela’s source reliability, engineering release, and rollback control. Finally, I will keep Owen’s and Ines’s Q4 development focuses open until the required December cycle is complete, then use the owner-reviewed evidence to decide what should carry forward into 2028.

Priya’s November 15 review comment has been incorporated: the opening now leads with Riley’s ownership of the bounded paid-batch operating frame and four-lane claim limits; Owen, Ines, and Daniela are credited explicitly; the exclusions cover pipeline and forecast treatment, early mature claims for the live cohort, and automatic expansion beyond the fifth consumer; and December development outcomes remain open.

arguments.body:
Evidence bank — year-end first-draft expansion

The clearest evidence of my 2027 contribution is not a broad growth claim; it is the bounded Helio Start proposal and the claim discipline I owned around it. I translated the opportunity into a controlled paid-search batch with explicit attribution safeguards, pause and stop conditions, and staffing and support-clock requirements. I also set the evidence boundary before launch: operating activity could be reported descriptively, but the new batch could not support mature customer-outcome claims until the fixed cohort had complete day-90 observation windows. I did not treat launch authorization as proof of effectiveness, and I did not authorize an additional paid batch by implication.

I own the proposal, the operating limits, and the language of the claims. Priya deserves explicit credit for approving the batch and the high-intent paid-search traffic. Daniela deserves explicit credit for the final November 1 launch authorization and for verifying the live enable control. Those approvals were essential to execution, but they are distinct from my ownership of the bounded design, attribution guardrails, stop conditions, support coverage requirements, and evidence limits.

The current paid batch should be described as live operational work, not mature evidence. The November 10 support-monitor evaluation recorded 23 paid-source eligibility-flow starts; attribution reconciled for all 23, with 7 reaching the assisted route and 10 reaching the admitted route. These are useful operating observations about routing and instrumentation. They are not a mature outcome read, not a causal acquisition result, and not evidence of downstream retention, revenue, or scale. The fixed cohort still needs complete day-90 windows before those claims can be considered.

Four-lane year-end evidence framing

1. Helio Start customer outcomes. This lane covers the bounded proposal, admissions, activation and downstream outcome windows, with paid-source attribution kept separate from outcome interpretation. My exclusions are explicit: no mature outcome claim for the November batch before complete day-90 windows; no causal, revenue, pipeline, acquisition-efficiency, scale, or forecast claim from live-batch counts; and no assumption that admitted or assisted routing is equivalent to successful customer value.

2. Expansion Assist. This remains a distinct lane from Helio Start setup and lifecycle work. The framing is limited to the certified source, denominator, outcome-window, and operating evidence actually available. I exclude combining Expansion Assist with Helio Start to create a larger or cleaner-looking result, and I exclude unsupported causal or business-impact claims where the source only supports descriptive operating facts.

3. Pricing-page path quality. This lane is about path quality and unsupported-path starts, not a general conversion or growth claim. I exclude treating path-quality continuity as proof of incremental revenue, pipeline, acquisition performance, or causal lift. Any conclusion must preserve the applicable denominator, period, and the distinction between a cleaner route and a downstream customer outcome.

4. System controls and reliability. This lane covers governed-state consumption, send or suppress behavior, source integrity, release controls, rollback readiness, and exception handling. I exclude turning reliable control behavior into a claim of customer or financial impact without a separate outcome source. I also keep release readiness, operational safety, and message-state correctness visibly separate from the three customer or path-quality lanes.

This four-lane framing is also an exclusion mechanism: each lane keeps its own owner, denominator, source completeness, outcome window, reliability evidence, and unresolved gaps. I do not fill a missing field in one lane with a result from another, and I do not convert an operational checkpoint into a closed year-end conclusion.

Delegated evidence and operating leadership

Owen's work strengthened the measurement layer behind the claims. He owned the denominator and measurement work, normalized what counted in each read, checked source completeness, and reconciled exceptions rather than allowing them to disappear into an aggregate. His exception synthesis distinguishes missing required input from other exception categories, and routine source-completeness closure depends on the required named-owner certifications and the absence of a disputed semantic or cross-surface discrepancy. This is an important example of leadership through delegation: I retained the final claim and exclusion decisions while Owen made the underlying evidence more auditable and decision-ready.

Owen's October–December Q4 development focus remains open through the December cycle. The November synthesis is evidence of progress, not permission to mark the focus complete early. The remaining assessment should use the required December cycle and preserve the same standards for denominator clarity, source completeness, and exception classification.

Ines strengthened lifecycle governance and message-state consumption. Her lane covers state transitions, routine-send controls, governed lifecycle interpretation, and audits within the established operating ceiling. The operating rule is fail closed when required state is missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting: a record is held rather than treated as queued delivery, and every possible display receives a fresh evaluation under the current governed state. This is the control logic that keeps a lifecycle message from outrunning the state it is supposed to represent.

The incomplete-setup reminder is the fifth production consumer of the shared-state feed, not a sixth consumer. In the November 1–7 operating read, the fully released reminder had 12,480 fresh evaluations, including 186 evaluations held because required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting. Those figures are evidence of the control operating as designed, not a claim of customer impact. The reminder's behavior belongs in the shared-state and reliability framing: it consumes governed state, can be placed on hold, and must be re-evaluated after state changes. It should not be counted as an unrelated extra system or used to inflate a customer-outcome result.

Ines's October–December Q4 development focus also remains open through the December cycle. Her demonstrated lifecycle-risk explanations and state-governance work are meaningful progress, but they do not close the development focus before the required December review. I will keep that assessment open rather than turning partial-cycle evidence into a completion claim.

Daniela's evidence covers source reliability, engineering release control, source-integrity validation, production enablement, rollback readiness, and incident-stop execution. That work made the bounded launch operable and gave the team a safe way to stop or reverse it if the source, release, or operating conditions failed. Her November 1 authorization is therefore part of the launch record, while the resulting paid-batch activity remains operational evidence pending the outcome window. I credit her for the reliability, release, and rollback work without attributing those engineering controls to mature customer or business results.

Year-end claim discipline

My role this year was to connect growth proposals to an evidence system without letting urgency erase the boundaries. The strongest version of the self-review should say that I created a bounded path to learn, secured the necessary approvals, and kept the language proportional to what the data can currently support. It should credit Priya, Daniela, Owen, and Ines for their distinct contributions; preserve the four lanes and their exclusions; call the paid batch live operational work rather than mature evidence; and leave Owen's and Ines's Q4 development focuses open through the December cycle.

Owen Pham owned measurement, reporting semantics, and exception reporting. Ines Kovac owned lifecycle governance and message-state work. Daniela owned source reliability, engineering release, and rollback control. That separation is an operating-model result in itself: each decision was supported by the appropriate owner evidence rather than by a blended claim.

Evidence and claim discipline

I have been deliberate about distinguishing what was decided, what was observed, and what remains unproven. The November 1–7 reminder operation had 12,480 fresh evaluations. Of those, 1,615 displayed, 520 were suppressed because current Customer Success work was active, 186 were held because required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting, and 10,159 did not display because current setup or qualifying-human-admin conditions were not met. These are operating counts, not claims of customer impact, durable behavior change, or mature performance.

The paid-batch evidence is similarly bounded. By Owen’s November 5 operating snapshot, 12 paid-source eligibility-flow starts had reached final states: five admitted, four assisted, and three ineligible, with $1,580 in spend. Paid-source attribution reconciled through every final route, and no unsupported applicant entered the admitted path. This is a live operating-status read, not a mature-outcome read. The formal support-pause monitor had not begun because the admission count was still below its threshold. I will continue to avoid converting early routing and control evidence into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale.

The evidence boundary also requires acknowledging what did not occur during the November 1–7 reminder interval: no reusable audience was created, no failed rollback occurred, no incident stop was triggered, and no customer correction was recorded. Those facts demonstrate the bounded state of the operation; they do not prove that the system is broadly mature or that future intervals will behave the same way.

Team development

My leadership goal has been to make ownership legible and to develop independent operating judgment without absorbing other people’s lanes. Owen’s measurement and exception-reporting work includes definitions, denominators, bounded operating snapshots, and exception synthesis. Ines’s work includes lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, lifecycle-risk explanation, and message-state transitions and controls. Daniela’s work includes source-integrity and reliability checks, production enablement, engineering release control, and rollback readiness.

The Q4 development focuses for Owen and Ines remain open through the required December cycle. October and November submissions are evidence of progress, not completion of the October–December focus. Owen’s November operating read and Ines’s November lifecycle-risk explanation should be credited to their respective lanes, while the focus remains open until the required December cycle is completed and reviewed. I am preserving that status rather than prematurely marking either development focus complete. I likewise continue to keep Daniela’s engineering authority intact rather than treating my operating decisions as a substitute for release or rollback ownership.

System reliability

The reliability improvement I helped drive was procedural as much as technical: explicit gates, fresh state evaluation, held-versus-queued semantics, active-work suppression, staffed backup handling, and a clear stop/correction boundary. The November paid batch launched only after the control evidence was available. Daniela verified the live enable and rollback controls and retained engineering authority. Ines maintained the lifecycle and message-state boundary. Owen provided the bounded measurement and exception read. The reminder operation’s agreed reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes show that the five-consumer operation remained coherent during the observed interval.

I do not interpret the absence of a failed rollback, incident stop, or customer correction as proof that reliability work is finished. The right claim is narrower: the controls were exercised in a bounded live interval without those recorded events, and the owner lanes and escalation boundaries held. Continued operation and the required December cycle are still needed before making broader claims.

Next-cycle focus

In the next cycle, I will continue to make explicit, reversible operating decisions with approval gates and evidence boundaries visible in the working record. I want to improve the handoff from live operating status to a genuinely mature outcome read: clear thresholds, complete observation windows, denominator discipline, and an explicit decision about when evidence is sufficient for expansion, continuation, or pause.

I will keep the five-consumer reminder operation within its current shared-state contract while reviewing held, suppressed, and displayed paths for operational clarity rather than optimizing display volume. I will also preserve the distinction between my decision lane and the owner lanes: Owen’s measurement and exception synthesis, Ines’s lifecycle governance and message-state work, and Daniela’s source reliability, engineering release, and rollback control. Finally, I will keep Owen’s and Ines’s Q4 development focuses open until the required December cycle is complete, then use the owner-reviewed evidence to decide what should carry forward into 2028.

arguments.title: Q4 investigation readout guidance — lightweight trial
arguments.body:
Q4 investigation readout guidance — lightweight trial

This is Q4 guidance, not a companywide mandatory template. Use it as a lightweight trial to make investigation readouts easier to review without creating a new process for people to police.

Lightweight checklist
- State the question, audience, and decision the investigation informs.
- Show the relevant comparison, population, timing, and effect size before the conclusion.
- Separate observed results from interpretation and next steps.
- Mark uncertainty, notable cuts, and lifecycle or instrumentation risks.
- Do not call a result significant until the stabilization-cohort boundary is met; first significance waits for one stabilization cohort.
- Keep the readout short and link supporting detail rather than expanding the main document.

Review prompts
- Is the standard readout shape clear and easy to scan? Owen reviews.
- Does the lifecycle-risk language distinguish risk, evidence, and action without overstating the finding? Ines reviews.
- Does the effect size appear before the conclusion?
- Is the first-significance / stabilization-cohort boundary explicit?
- What feels unclear or overly heavy after initial use?

Follow-up: collect lightweight feedback after the first uses and decide whether any wording needs adjustment.

arguments.title: Renewal-risk readout — reordered around denominator and observed outcome
arguments.body:
Renewal-risk readout — January 13, 2025

Purpose

Reorder the Customer Success readout around the population reviewed, the observed outcome, and the limits of what the evidence can support. This preserves the lightweight investigation framework as a readout practice; it does not create an approval queue or turn every readout into a mandatory signoff process.

1. Cohort and denominator

- Cohort: September renewal cohort, paid accounts in the 75–200-seat segment.
- Complete review population: 342 accounts.
- Comparison groups, defined by observed behavior through day 10:
  - 216 accounts had invited a teammate.
  - 126 accounts had not invited a teammate.
- These groups are descriptive exposure/status groups, not randomized treatment arms.

2. Observed outcome

- Retention among accounts with a teammate invited by day 10: 82.1%.
- Retention among accounts without a teammate invited by day 10: 79.8%.
- Observed difference: +2.3 percentage points for the teammate-invited group.
- Statistical read: p=.047 on the first significant read.
- Add the corresponding retention numerators beside these denominators in the circulated version so the rates are auditable.

3. Careful interpretation

The observed data show a retention difference between the two groups. They do not establish that inviting a teammate caused higher retention. Invite behavior was observed rather than randomized, so the difference may partly reflect healthier, more engaged, or otherwise different accounts being more likely to invite teammates. The first significant read is preliminary and should not be presented as a durable stabilization result, a causal effect, or evidence that a reminder will improve renewal.

Remove or rewrite any opening sentence that attributes the retention difference to teammate invitations. Open with the 342-account denominator and the observed retention comparison instead.

4. Investigation status and bounded next step

- Keep the finding in the readout as an investigation signal.
- A reminder remains a bounded test hypothesis, not a launch or ship recommendation.
- The next cohort should be used to assess whether the signal stabilizes before any send decision.
- If a test is later proposed, define the holdout, eligibility, timing, cadence, copy, exclusions, and success/guardrail measures in the test plan.

5. Proposed audience, only as a hypothesis for review

The previously proposed audience was:

- No teammate invited by day 10.
- No open Customer Success adoption plan.
- No Support contact in the prior 14 days.
- Active admin activity in the prior 7 days.

Keep this as a candidate audience for review, not an approved send audience. It needs lifecycle-risk assessment for whether the message could feel like renewal pressure, plus confirmation that current-state suppression is accurate at exposure time.

6. Lightweight operating lanes

- Owen owns denominator visibility, effect-size framing, and conclusion order. This is a quality lane for the readout shape, not approval of every individual readout.
- Ines owns lifecycle recommendation QA and audience-risk caveats, including suppression, pressure risk, timing, cadence, copy, and any holdout considerations when a lifecycle action is actually proposed.
- Customer Success owns the account context and readout draft.
- Riley retains judgment on higher-risk or cross-functional decisions, but the framework does not turn routine readouts into an approval queue.

7. What this readout does not claim

- No causal claim that teammate invitations drive renewal.
- No durable effect claim from the first significant read.
- No broad reminder approval or send authorization.
- No conclusion that the proposed audience is safe merely because it is narrower than the first draft.
- No companywide mandatory template or new approval process.

Bottom line

Among 342 paid 75–200-seat September renewal accounts, 216 had invited a teammate by day 10 and 126 had not; observed retention was 82.1% versus 79.8%, a +2.3-point difference, with p=.047 on the first significant read. This is a preliminary descriptive association. Keep it as a bounded investigation signal, seek a stabilization read, and preserve the lightweight denominator/effect-size/conclusion-order practice without converting it into an approval queue.

Owner lanes

input.body:
Purpose

Use this checklist before designing any new Growth or Customer Success lifecycle decisioning, including eligibility, routing, reminders, assisted paths, admissions, holds, or measurement changes.

Decision rule

Design may proceed only after every item marked “Required before design” is satisfied and evidenced. If any required prerequisite is missing, design must not proceed beyond intake and clarification. You may document the problem, gather evidence, and draft questions; do not create solution flows, states, triggers, copy, instrumentation, or implementation-ready specs until the prerequisite is satisfied.

Intake record

- Request name and owner:
- Requesting team: Growth / Customer Success / shared
- Date received:
- Desired launch or decision date:
- Decisioning surface(s):
- Executive or accountable approver:
- Product/design owner:
- Data/analytics owner:
- Operations or Customer Success owner:
- Engineering owner:

1. Problem and outcome

- What user or business problem is being addressed?
- Who is affected, and who is explicitly out of scope?
- What user action or business outcome should change?
- Why is this being addressed now?
- What is the expected value, risk reduction, or operational benefit?
- What is the smallest decision that must be made?

Prerequisite: A bounded problem statement, target population, intended outcome, and explicit out-of-scope boundaries are written and approved by the accountable owner.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No. Without this, design would be solving an unbounded or potentially different problem.
Evidence: Approved intake statement or ticket link.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

2. Decision authority and governance

- Who owns the decision policy?
- Who may approve exceptions, overrides, and launch?
- Are Legal, Privacy, Security, Compliance, Finance, or Support reviews required?
- Are there contractual, regulatory, accessibility, or consent constraints?
- What is the escalation path when data or policy conflicts?

Prerequisite: A named accountable policy owner and a documented review/approval path exist.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No. A flow cannot be designed responsibly when authority, constraints, or escalation rights are unknown.
Evidence: Owner list, policy reference, and review matrix.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

3. Source-of-truth policy and definitions

- What is the authoritative policy or business rule?
- Define every key term, including eligible, ineligible, qualified, active, stale, held, queued, sent, admitted, assisted, converted, suppressed, and completed.
- Identify conflicting definitions across Growth, Customer Success, Product, Operations, and Analytics.
- Specify whether the requested behavior is a new rule, a change to an existing rule, or a measurement-only change.
- Record effective dates, version, and known exceptions.

Prerequisite: The authoritative rule set and a glossary of decision states and exceptions are approved, with conflicts resolved or explicitly escalated.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No. Design must not invent semantics or silently reconcile conflicting definitions.
Evidence: Versioned policy, glossary, and decision-state register.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

4. Population, eligibility, and exclusions

- Identify the population entering the lifecycle.
- Define eligibility inputs, required fields, freshness rules, and evaluation timing.
- Define exclusions, suppression, consent, regional, plan, account, and lifecycle restrictions.
- State whether evaluation is one-time, event-driven, scheduled, or re-evaluated at each display/opportunity.
- Define behavior when data is missing, stale, contradictory, or late.
- Identify re-entry, duplicate, merge, and cross-device/account behavior.

Prerequisite: Eligibility, exclusions, data-quality behavior, evaluation timing, and re-entry rules are complete enough to classify every in-scope case.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No. Unclassified cases create unsafe gaps and inconsistent user treatment.
Evidence: Eligibility matrix and sample cases, including missing/stale/contradictory data.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

5. Lifecycle states and transitions

- List all states, entry criteria, exit criteria, and terminal states.
- Define every allowed transition and the event or actor that causes it.
- Specify hold, pause, retry, expiration, cancellation, reactivation, and manual override behavior.
- Distinguish decision evaluation from delivery eligibility, queued delivery, actual delivery, and user completion.
- Define idempotency and duplicate-event handling.
- Identify state ownership and the system of record.

Prerequisite: A complete state-transition model exists, including failure, hold, retry, and manual paths.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No. A partial state model cannot support reliable UX, operations, or measurement design.
Evidence: State table or transition diagram reviewed by Product, Operations, and Engineering.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

6. Experience and channel inventory

- Inventory every affected surface, channel, CTA, message, notification, workflow, and assisted route.
- Document where a user can start, resume, abandon, or be redirected.
- Identify self-serve versus assisted experiences and who owns each route.
- Define precedence when multiple prompts, journeys, or channels qualify at once.
- Check localization, accessibility, frequency caps, quiet hours, and support readiness.
- Identify existing behavior that must remain unchanged.

Prerequisite: The complete cross-surface and cross-channel inventory is known, including assisted paths and precedence rules.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No for solution design. Discovery of the inventory may proceed, but implementation-ready design may not.
Evidence: Surface/channel map and collision-precedence rules.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

7. Data, instrumentation, and measurement contract

- State the primary success metric and guardrail metrics.
- Define the denominator, population window, attribution rule, and reporting grain.
- Separate eligibility-flow starts, setup-help or assisted-CTA clicks, admissions, assisted routes, deliveries, and downstream outcomes where applicable.
- Define event names, properties, timestamps, identity keys, deduplication, and source of truth.
- Specify how holds, suppressions, missing data, retries, and reassessments are counted.
- Define baseline, target, experiment/control requirements, and stop conditions.

Prerequisite: Analytics has approved a measurement contract that makes each required state and outcome observable without ambiguous counting.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No for final flow or instrumentation design. Exploratory discovery may proceed only if clearly labeled non-final.
Evidence: Metric definitions, event schema, dashboard/report owner, and baseline availability.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

8. Operational readiness and ownership

- Who monitors the lifecycle and its queues?
- Who handles holds, exceptions, appeals, retries, and user questions?
- What service levels and handoff rules apply?
- What tools, permissions, templates, and runbooks are required?
- What happens if a downstream system, provider, or integration is unavailable?
- How are stale records identified and re-evaluated?

Prerequisite: Operations and Customer Success have accepted ownership, exception handling, service levels, and runbook requirements.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No for a launchable design. A conceptual exploration may proceed, but it must not be presented as deployable.
Evidence: RACI, exception matrix, runbook owner, and support sign-off.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

9. Technical feasibility and dependencies

- Identify systems of record, APIs, event sources, jobs, queues, permissions, and integrations.
- Confirm data availability, latency, retention, and reliability.
- Identify migration, backfill, feature-flag, experiment, and rollback needs.
- Record known platform constraints and dependency owners.
- Define failure modes and safe defaults.
- Confirm that proposed states and events can be persisted and replayed or audited as needed.

Prerequisite: Engineering has confirmed feasibility, dependencies, constraints, and a safe rollback or disable path.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: Limited discovery may proceed; implementation-ready or feasibility-dependent design may not.
Evidence: Technical assessment, dependency list, and rollback plan.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

10. Risk, privacy, accessibility, and harm review

- Identify risks from false eligibility, missed eligibility, unwanted contact, exclusion, or repeated prompting.
- Check consent, personal data minimization, retention, access, and audit requirements.
- Consider vulnerable users, accessibility needs, language, geography, and equitable treatment.
- Define human review and appeal paths where automated decisions can materially affect users.
- Record residual risks, mitigations, and accepted-risk owner.

Prerequisite: Required risk and compliance reviews are complete, or the accountable reviewers have documented the constraints under which design may proceed.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No if the unresolved issue could change the decision rule, population, data use, or user safety. Only non-binding exploration may proceed.
Evidence: Review record, risk register, mitigations, and approvals.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

11. Test cases and acceptance criteria

- Provide representative happy paths and boundary cases.
- Include eligible, ineligible, missing, stale, contradictory, held, retried, suppressed, duplicate, re-entering, and manually overridden cases.
- Include simultaneous qualifications, channel collisions, failure recovery, and assisted handoff cases.
- Define expected state, user experience, event emission, operational action, and metric effect for each case.
- Define launch acceptance thresholds and post-launch verification checks.

Prerequisite: The accountable owners have approved testable acceptance criteria covering all material states and exception paths.
Design may proceed before this is satisfied: No. Without acceptance criteria, design cannot be verified against policy or operational reality.
Evidence: Scenario matrix and signed acceptance criteria.
Status: [ ] Satisfied  [ ] Blocked  [ ] N/A

12. Intake decision and design gate

- [ ] All required prerequisites above are satisfied or an explicit exception is approved.
- [ ] Open questions are assigned to named owners with due dates.
- [ ] Any approved exceptions state scope, risk, expiration, and compensating control.
- [ ] The design brief repeats the approved definitions, states, metrics, and constraints.

Gate outcome:

[ ] Proceed to design — all required prerequisites are satisfied.
[ ] Proceed only with non-binding discovery — one or more prerequisites remain open; no implementation-ready artifacts.
[ ] Do not proceed — an unresolved blocker affects policy, safety, authority, population, state semantics, or measurement validity.

Decision owner:
Decision date:
Open blockers:
Approved exceptions:
Next review date:

Minimum evidence pack

- Approved problem statement and scope
- Named decision owner and review matrix
- Versioned policy, glossary, and exceptions
- Eligibility and exclusion matrix
- Complete state-transition model
- Surface/channel and assisted-route inventory
- Measurement contract and event schema
- Operational RACI and exception runbook
- Technical feasibility and rollback assessment
- Risk/compliance/accessibility review
- Scenario matrix and acceptance criteria

Reusable operating principle

Do not design around missing definitions. Make the missing prerequisite visible, assign an owner, and keep the work at discovery level until the decision can be expressed, implemented, operated, measured, and reviewed consistently across every affected surface.

arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — H1 2027 self-review

In H1, I shifted routine execution toward accountable owners while keeping my involvement focused on exceptions, decision boundaries, and control quality. The result was greater operating leverage without weakening accountability: the team could carry work through its normal path, while I remained responsible for the system, the evidence standard, and the higher-order decisions that depend on it.

Operating model: January incomplete-packet handling

A concrete example came in January, when a routine four-lane packet was incomplete. The sanitized campaign snapshot did not include the required owner-certified year-end export. Rather than use stale data or treat the missing certification as a waiver, Owen identified the blocker and escalated the packet for exception review. I reviewed the exception and clarified the required path, but did not take routine preparation back or become the default operator.

Once the certified export arrived, the work returned to its accountable lanes. Ines completed the lifecycle-governance and owner-state certification. Daniela completed source-reliability and release certification. Owen closed the snapshot with the delay documented and resolved. This was the operating model working as intended: ownership stayed with the people closest to the work, escalation was evidence-based, and my intervention was proportional to the risk rather than a substitute for execution.

I reinforced this approach through exception-only involvement and a deliberate quarterly hands-on audit. The audit was a check of the operating system, evidence, and escalation paths in practice—not a return to day-to-day ownership. It helped me test whether delegation was functioning, detect drift, and intervene where the controls or decision quality warranted it.

Decision boundary: Helio Start paid test

The Q2 Helio Start paid test provided a second example, this time of bounded decision-making. I set and governed explicit admission, spend, cohort, and stop boundaries before launch. The test launched within those guardrails and closed in May at the 25-workspace admission cap, after $7,640 in spend against an $8,000 ceiling. The 61 starts reconciled to one final state: 25 admitted, 18 assisted, and 18 ineligible. At close, traffic was turned off, the cohort was fixed, and no later batch or cap extension was authorized.

My decision was to hold the boundary at close rather than reopen traffic or admit another workspace simply because demand remained available. Owen’s lane was routine paid-source ownership and execution within the approved bounds. Ines’s lane was lifecycle governance, including the applicable lifecycle rules, review, and escalation path. Daniela’s lane was engineering control: routing, instrumentation, and technical safeguards. Their execution ownership was important to the test, but it did not transfer my authority over causal interpretation, revenue claims, forecast treatment, board readiness, or executive-language decisions.

Evidence boundary

The closed test establishes that we could execute and reconcile a bounded paid-source experiment at the approved cap and spend, with the observed admission mix and no detected attribution, routing, or instrumentation failure requiring a pause. It provides useful descriptive operating information and an initial support signal. It does not, before complete day-90 windows, establish mature retention, expansion, payback, long-term product value, durable unit economics, causal paid-source performance, revenue contribution, forecast credit, or a board-ready conclusion.

Mature paid-active status, refund-adjusted cash, and mature account-level support effort remain unavailable pending complete day-90 windows. I am therefore treating the result as a disciplined test and an evidence boundary, not as a premature scale recommendation.

Team development and growth edge

I made ownership explicit, separated routine execution from exception handling, and gave the team visible guardrails and evidence-based escalation paths. That reduced role overlap and improved decision traceability while preserving my accountability for system quality and higher-order interpretation.

My development edge is to leave owner-ready work with its owner. I can improve by resisting the urge to pull a complete, well-bounded deliverable back into my lane for polishing or reassurance. My job is to set the standard, make the decision boundary and review point clear, and intervene when evidence or risk warrants it. Allowing accountable owners to carry work through completion will preserve leverage without implying that delegation transfers my causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, or executive-language authority.

Closing

My H1 contribution was a shift from broad routine operation to higher-leverage system ownership: I clarified decision rights, handled exceptions without reclaiming execution, audited the model deliberately, and governed a bounded paid test through launch and close without over-claiming what the evidence could support. In the next half, I will sharpen evidence timing and decision records while continuing to let owner-ready work remain with its owner.

input.body:
Effective 2028-01-01

Purpose
Keep routine framework maintenance moving without routing every change to the framework sponsor. Teams should use the ownership paths below for standard updates and escalate only material scope, policy, or risk decisions.

Ownership and routing

- Readout shape and templates — Readout Operations owns the canonical structure, field names, section order, and formatting guidance. Route proposed standard-shape changes there for review and incorporation.
- Examples and sample investigations — Domain teams own examples in their area; Readout Operations checks that examples still match the canonical shape. Route additions, corrections, and replacements to the relevant domain team, copying Readout Operations when the example changes the pattern.
- Lifecycle-risk content — Lifecycle/Risk Operations owns risk definitions, stage gates, warning indicators, controls, and escalation language. Route changes here for impact and control review before publication.
- Cross-cutting framework stewardship — Framework Steward maintains the source of truth, changelog, versioning, and release notes; resolves overlaps between owners and publishes approved updates.
- Sponsor escalation — Send only decisions that change investigation scope, accountability, approval thresholds, external commitments, or risk posture to the framework sponsor.

Default handling

1. The receiving owner confirms whether the request is routine, cross-cutting, or sponsor-level.
2. Routine changes are edited, reviewed, and logged by the receiving owner.
3. Changes affecting both readout structure/examples and lifecycle risk receive parallel review from both owners before release.
4. The Framework Steward publishes the approved version and records the rationale, effective date, and owner.
5. If ownership is unclear, route to the Framework Steward—not directly to the sponsor.

Minimum request details

Include the proposed text or example, affected section/stage, reason for change, evidence or source, requested effective date, and any backward-compatibility or reporting impact.

# Mid-seg churn spike — H2 ruling: seasonal / competitor cycle

## Ruling
H2 is ruled out as the explanation for the current mid-segment churn spike. The same-week historical comparison does not show a prior version of the current spike, weakening both seasonal and competitor-cycle explanations.

## Evidence
- Current mid-segment monthly churn: 5.1%.
- February 2021 same-week mid-segment monthly churn: 2.0%.
- February 2022 same-week mid-segment monthly churn: 2.2%.
- Historical comparisons use the same cohort logic as the January scan.
- Owen's denominator-handling check found no cohort-definition or denominator issue that would explain the result.

## Interpretation
The current result is not a normal February pattern in the available historical comps. H2 is closed for this investigation; the remaining investigation should focus on the other hypothesis buckets rather than seasonal or competitor-cycle recurrence.

## Parallel work / contamination boundary
Marcus can continue running the pricing-page test separately. Its results should not be folded into this H2 ruling or treated as a validation of the churn-investigation conclusion.

## Method note
Retain the historical comps directly next to the ruling so the decision is auditable and does not get reframed as a “weird month” call without the comparison and cohort-definition context.

PRE-RULING ARTIFACT — HISTORICAL SNAPSHOT

Artifact date: 2028-01-01
Historical phase captured: 2023-02-17, before the H2 ruling
Status: Pre-ruling; H2 remains open and pending evidence. Do not read this artifact as the later H2 decision.

Investigation context
The validated 50–200-seat mid-segment cut was 5.1% monthly churn versus a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. Owen had rechecked the cut, so the working position was that this was not being treated as a cohort-definition error. The tiered pass was nearly flat—entry 5.0%, standard 5.2%, plus 5.1%—which downgraded pricing artifact as the primary explanation but did not by itself rule it out. Marcus’s pricing-page experiment was a separate parallel track and a contamination risk, not evidence for H2.

Active hypothesis: H2
The February mid-segment churn increase may be explained by a recurring seasonal pattern or a competitor cycle, rather than by a product/pricing artifact. The pre-ruling question was whether February represented a repeatable historical pattern and/or whether a segment-specific movement aligned with dated external events.

Planned historical comparison work
1. Use the same cohort logic as the established January scan and preserve Owen’s denominator-handling check.
2. Line up same-window monthly churn by segment across historical February windows, with the 50–200-seat mid-segment cut as the primary comparison.
3. Compare starter, mid_seg, growth, and enterprise where the source supports those cuts; keep the metric of record as monthly logo churn rate.
4. Overlay dated market events and only timestamped competitor activity that can be actually verified.
5. Keep Marcus’s pricing-page experiment separate so concurrent experiment exposure does not contaminate the historical H2 read.
6. Do not hand-wave the result as a “weird February” without the historical comparison; leave H2 pending until the source cuts and event log are available.

Decision standard for H2
Rule H2 in only if the same-window historical comparison shows a repeatable February pattern and/or a segment-specific movement that lines up with dated external events. Otherwise, rule H2 out. The pre-ruling artifact records the decision standard, not the eventual call.

Agreed one-pager operating model for every hypothesis ruling
Owner: Owen. Every hypothesis ruling—whether ruled in or ruled out—gets its own Owen-authored one-pager.

Required contents of each one-pager:
- Why: the rationale for testing the hypothesis and the relevant decision context.
- Cuts: the cohort, segment, time-window, denominator, and comparison cuts used; include the historical same-window cuts for H2.
- Statistical evidence: p-value and effect size, where applicable, with enough method/context to interpret them.
- Call: the explicit final ruling, in or out, plus the evidence-based interpretation and any remaining caveat or boundary.

Hypothesis-by-hypothesis ownership map
- H1 — Pricing artifact (packaging, discounting, or contract-mix effects): Owen owns the ruling one-pager; it must document why, pricing/contract-mix cuts, p-value/effect-size evidence, and the final call. Keep it separate from Marcus’s pricing-page experiment.
- H2 — Competitor cycle / seasonal pattern: Owen owns the ruling one-pager; it must document why, same-window historical monthly churn cuts by segment, dated market/competitor-event overlays, p-value/effect-size evidence, and the final call. At this snapshot, the H2 one-pager is planned, not complete.
- H3 — Onboarding timing: Owen owns the ruling one-pager; it must document why, start-date/cohort timing and lagged-churn cuts, p-value/effect-size evidence, and the final call.
- H4 — CS coverage gap: Owen owns the ruling one-pager; it must document why, CSM-load/coverage and affected-segment cuts, p-value/effect-size evidence, and the final call.

Pre-ruling guardrail
This artifact intentionally stops before the later H2 ruling. It preserves the active hypothesis, planned comparison, and documentation agreement as they stood in the pre-ruling phase; no later historical rates, competitor events, p-values, effect sizes, or ruling are backfilled here.

input.body:
Purpose

Historical review of Q4 2023 Expansion Assist shadow decisions for retained mid-segment accounts. Use this worksheet to reconstruct what was observed, apply the Customer Success suppression check used at the time, and determine whether the evidence combination was sufficient for a commercial prompt to be considered. This is an audit of shadow decisions—not a pipeline, forecast, launch approval, or retroactive Sales list.

Review scope and historical rule

- Population: retained mid-segment accounts surfaced by Q4 readiness heuristics.
- Core evidence combination required before a commercial prompt could be considered: (1) active-admin behavior, (2) deep integration use, and (3) product-visible usage-ceiling evidence.
- Interpretation: the three signals identify an interesting account but are not, by themselves, permission to prompt or hand off.
- Customer Success suppression check: if Customer Success adoption work, renewal work, onboarding/import work, or other active customer work was open, suppress the commercial prompt and record the account as not ready for commercial routing. The open work takes precedence over otherwise strong product signals.
- Missing active-admin behavior or shallow integration is an evidence gap/observational outcome, not a Sales-eligible classification.
- Usage-ceiling evidence without recent active-admin behavior is insufficient for the historical Expansion Assist classification.
- An old expansion quote requires a recheck before any commercial interpretation.
- Historical disposition should be recorded as shadow-only, suppressed, observational, evidence-gap, recheck-required, or (only if every gate is satisfied) prompt-consideration eligible. Do not infer that any row was actually sent to Sales.

Per-account audit worksheet

| # | Account / ID | Retained-mid confirmed? | Active-admin behavior (source/date) | Deep integration (source/date) | Product-visible usage ceiling (source/date) | All 3 present? | CS adoption / renewal / onboarding / import / other active work open? | Suppression result | Other evidence gap or recheck | Historical disposition | Reviewer / date | Source links or notes |

| 15 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 16 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 17 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| 18 |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

Decision procedure for each row

1. Confirm the account belongs to the retained mid-segment review population and preserve the original snapshot date.
2. Record source, timestamp, and exact observed value for each of the three evidence categories. Do not convert an inference into customer evidence.
3. Mark “All 3 present?” Yes only when active-admin behavior, deep integration, and product-visible usage-ceiling evidence are all independently supported.
4. Run the Customer Success suppression check against the same historical snapshot. Mark the check Failed/Suppress if any covered active work was open at that time. Record the work type, owner, status, and source.
5. Apply precedence: Suppress overrides the evidence combination. A suppressed row cannot be prompt-consideration eligible.
6. If not suppressed, classify the evidence state. Any missing active-admin behavior, shallow integration, unsupported ceiling, stale source, or old-quote dependency remains observational, evidence-gap, or recheck-required.
7. Only after steps 1–6 may a reviewer mark prompt-consideration eligible. This status means the row met the historical shadow criteria for consideration; it does not mean a prompt was issued or approved.
8. Record uncertainty and conflicting sources explicitly. Do not backfill later product or Customer Success state into the Q4 2023 decision.

Historical control totals and known outcomes

Use these as reconciliation checks. The groups are not necessarily mutually exclusive; do not add them together unless the source extract proves they are disjoint.

- 2023-11-28 limited shadow review population: 18 retained-mid accounts.
- Five of the 18 had the full active-admin + deep-integration + product-visible usage-ceiling combination.
- Six had usage-ceiling evidence but no recent active-admin behavior and were suppressed from the historical classification.
- Two had open Customer Success adoption plans; a commercial prompt would have collided with help already in progress.
- Four were described as commercially interesting but had open Customer Success adoption or import work and were suppressed.
- Customer Success reviewed seven November false positives; two were corrected.
- One renewal-risk row was suppressed.
- One row required an old expansion-quote recheck before any commercial interpretation.
- Final 2023-11-28 result: no Sales-facing rows. The review chose to refine state definitions, document evidence gaps, and decide what to observe next—not approve outreach or create a Sales list.
- Customer Success considered a monthly false-positive learning loop manageable, but not a weekly Sales pre-clear queue.

messages.content: [2023-12-11T10:34:00-06:00] Near the end of a four-mile easy run, my left calf got progressively tight. There was no pop, sharp pain, fall, bruising, swelling, numbness, or weakness, and I can walk normally, but the muscle feels sore when I rise onto my toes. I stopped running. Give me a conservative same-day triage plan and tell me what would make this more than ordinary muscle irritation, plus when it would be reasonable to test another run.

Based on what you described—gradual tightness, no pop, bruising, swelling, weakness, or walking difficulty—this sounds more consistent with mild calf muscle irritation or a low-grade strain than a major tear. It cannot be diagnosed remotely.

Same-day conservative plan

1. Stop running for the day. Walk normally only if it does not increase pain or make you limp. Avoid hills, stairs when avoidable, jumping, calf raises, and forceful stretching.

2. For the first 24–48 hours, use a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time, several times today. Do not apply ice directly to the skin.

3. Elevate the leg when resting. Gentle ankle pumps and easy ankle movements are reasonable if they are comfortable.

4. Compression can help if there is mild discomfort or swelling, but it should be light and comfortable. Remove it if you get numbness, tingling, increased pain, coolness, or color change.

5. Avoid deep massage, foam rolling, aggressive stretching, heat, and alcohol today; these can aggravate a fresh muscle injury.

6. If you need pain relief, acetaminophen is generally the simpler option if you can take it safely. Follow the label and avoid it with significant liver disease or heavy alcohol use. Ask a clinician or pharmacist before using ibuprofen or naproxen if you have kidney disease, ulcers, blood thinners, pregnancy, or other relevant contraindications.

Contact a clinician today or seek urgent evaluation if you develop:

- New or increasing one-sided calf swelling, warmth, redness, or marked tenderness
- Pain that is worsening at rest or becomes severe
- A pop, visible dent, bruising, or sudden loss of strength
- Inability to walk normally, push off, or perform a gentle single-leg heel raise
- Numbness, tingling, weakness, or a foot that becomes pale, blue, or cold
- Severe tightness or pain out of proportion to what happened
- Shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing blood, faintness, or a rapid heartbeat—call emergency services immediately

A blood clot is less suggested by your exercise-related gradual onset and absence of swelling, but new unilateral swelling, warmth, redness, or unexplained calf pain warrants prompt medical assessment, especially after recent immobilization or travel, prior clot, cancer, estrogen use, pregnancy/postpartum status, or a clotting disorder.

When to test another run

Do not test tomorrow merely because walking feels better. Wait until:

- You can walk briskly and use stairs without pain or a limp
- Calf stretching and ankle movement are nearly symptom-free
- You can do about 20 controlled single-leg heel raises and several gentle hops without pain, weakness, or protective movement
- The calf is no worse the following morning

For a mild episode, that may be roughly 48–72 hours, but it could take longer. Your first test should be 10–15 minutes on a flat route at clearly easy effort—about half your usual duration or distance. Stop immediately for sharp or escalating pain, renewed tightening, altered gait, weakness, or pain that changes your stride. If it passes, reassess later that day and the next morning before increasing duration; do not increase both speed and distance on the next run.

results.title: Manage mild calf tightness safely
results.snippet: Based on what you described—gradual mild tightness after >>>running<<<, no pop, normal walking and calf raise, and no swelling or systemic symptoms—this is reasonably managed as a minor calf irritation for now. It cannot be diagnosed remotely, though...

messages.content: [2024-03-09T09:30:00-06:00] After a five-mile run this morning I have mild tightness in the middle of my right calf, maybe a 2 out of 10. There wasn't a pop or sudden pain, I can walk normally and do a calf raise, and I don't have swelling, bruising, warmth, or shortness of breath. I want to avoid turning a minor irritation into a real injury. What conservative same-day care and activity guidance makes sense, and what's the clear line where I should stop self-care and get medical advice?

Based on what you described—gradual mild tightness after running, no pop, normal walking and calf raise, and no swelling or systemic symptoms—this is reasonably managed as a minor calf irritation for now. It cannot be diagnosed remotely, though.

Same-day care

- Stop running for the rest of today. Avoid hills, speed work, jumping, and heavy calf-strength work.
- Normal walking is fine if it does not increase the pain or cause a limp. Keep it easy and minimize unnecessary walking.
- Use a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 10–15 minutes at a time if it feels helpful, repeating every few hours today. Do not apply ice directly to the skin.
- Elevate the leg when resting. Light, comfortable compression is optional; remove it if you get numbness, tingling, increased pain, coolness, or color change.
- Do gentle ankle pumps and circles within a comfortable range. Do not aggressively stretch, massage, foam-roll, or “test” the calf repeatedly today.
- If you need pain relief, acetaminophen according to the label is a conservative option. Ibuprofen or another anti-inflammatory may be reasonable only if you normally can take it safely and have no relevant kidney, stomach-bleeding, anticoagulant, allergy, or pregnancy concerns.

For the next 24–48 hours, use symptoms as the guide. Mild discomfort that stays stable or improves during easy walking is more reassuring; pain that escalates during activity or is worse the next morning means you did too much.

Do not try another run until you can briskly walk and use stairs without pain or a limp, move the ankle and gently stretch the calf nearly symptom-free, and perform controlled single-leg heel raises without pain or weakness. Your first test should be short, flat, and easy—roughly 10–15 minutes—and stopped immediately for sharp or increasing pain, renewed tightening, weakness, or any change in your stride.

Get urgent medical advice promptly—same day or sooner—if you develop:

- Increasing one-sided calf swelling, warmth, redness, or marked tenderness
- Pain that becomes significant at rest or progressively worsens despite resting
- A pop, sudden sharp pain, visible indentation, substantial bruising, or inability to walk, push off, or do a gentle heel raise
- Numbness, tingling, weakness, or a pale, blue, or cold foot
- Calf symptoms without a clear exercise explanation, particularly after recent immobilization, long travel, surgery, prior clot, cancer, or hormone use

Call emergency services for shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing blood, fainting, or sudden unexplained rapid breathing. If the mild tightness is not clearly improving within 48–72 hours, or remains limiting after about a week, arrange a clinician or sports-medicine evaluation.

messages.content: [2024-05-11T09:14:00-05:00] During a four-mile Saturday run, I developed a mild ache along the outside of my right ankle in the final mile. There was no twist, fall, pop, or sudden pain. I can bear weight normally, have no visible swelling or bruising, and the discomfort is around 2 out of 10 when descending stairs. I stopped rather than adding distance. Give me conservative self-care and return-to-running guidance, including whether I should skip my next run and what specific signs would justify prompt medical evaluation.

The absence of a twist, pop, swelling, bruising, or difficulty bearing weight is reassuring, but an outside-ankle ache can still represent an irritated tendon or muscle—and less commonly a bone stress injury.

Skip your next run. The fact that stairs still cause discomfort means the ankle has not yet passed an everyday activity test.

For the next 24–48 hours:

- Use relative rest: normal walking is reasonable if it does not increase pain or cause a limp. Avoid running, hills, jumping, and uneven surfaces.
- Ice is optional: 10–15 minutes with a cloth barrier, several times per day, especially if it feels soothing. Do not apply ice directly to skin.
- Elevate when resting. A light compression sleeve or elastic wrap is acceptable if comfortable; loosen it if you develop numbness, tingling, color change, or increased pain.
- Wear supportive, comfortable shoes. Avoid barefoot walking or unsupportive shoes if those aggravate it.
- Gentle ankle range-of-motion movements are fine if nearly pain-free. Do not force stretching, massage, or strengthening through pain.
- If needed, acetaminophen or an anti-inflammatory medicine may help if you normally can take it safely and follow the label. Avoid using medication to conceal pain so you can run.

You can try a gradual return only when all of these are true:

- Brisk walking and stairs are pain-free, without a limp.
- Ankle motion is nearly normal and comfortable.
- You can do about 20 controlled single-leg heel raises without pain, weakness, or wobbling.
- You can perform several gentle hops in place without pain.
- Symptoms are not worse later that day or the following morning.

First test run:

- Use a flat route and an easy effort.
- Run/walk for 10–15 minutes, roughly half your usual distance or duration.
- Stop immediately for sharp or increasing pain, renewed tightening, weakness, altered gait, or pain that changes your stride.
- Leave at least a day between early test runs. If symptoms remain stable during the run and are no worse the next morning, increase gradually—one factor at a time, preferably by about 10–20%.

Arrange prompt medical evaluation if:

- Pain becomes progressively worse, occurs at rest or at night, or is not clearly improving after several days.
- You develop focal tenderness directly over an ankle bone, the base of the fifth metatarsal on the outer foot, or another very specific bony spot.
- Swelling, bruising, warmth, redness, instability, or recurrent “giving way” appears.
- You cannot walk normally, push off, stand on the affected toes, or perform heel raises.
- You develop numbness, tingling, marked weakness, or a cold/pale/blue foot.
- Symptoms persist beyond roughly 1–2 weeks despite backing off.

Seek urgent care for a deformity, inability to bear weight, severe sudden pain, rapidly increasing swelling, or significant redness/warmth with fever. Emergency evaluation is warranted for new one-sided calf swelling and pain accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing blood, or faintness.

- Sharp, focal, or localized pain
- A limp, altered stride, weakness, wobbling, or a feeling of instability
- Pain that does not settle promptly after stopping

After stopping, skip further jogging and use pain-free walking or easy cycling only. Step back from running if symptoms recur with ordinary walking or stairs, or if the ankle is worse later that day or the next morning.
