arguments.title: Q1 lifecycle QA contractor — kickoff and handoff
arguments.body:
Q1 lifecycle QA contractor — kickoff and handoff

Owner: Ines
Engagement: Lifecycle QA and operations contractor
Dates: January 15–February 23, 2024 (six weeks)
Workspace: Growth

Purpose

Create a repeatable, evidence-based QA inventory and operating process for Customer.io lifecycle campaigns and templates. The contractor should document current behavior, test the highest-risk lifecycle cases, surface ownership and suppression gaps, and leave behind records that another person can rerun without relying on undocumented context.

Working principles

- Observe and document before proposing changes.
- Do not change production exposure, campaign logic, audience definitions, or Helio Start exposure as part of this engagement unless separately authorized in writing.
- Record evidence for every conclusion: link, screenshot, query/export, test workspace, timestamp, and reviewer where applicable.
- Treat unknown ownership, missing suppression logic, non-repeatable preflight steps, and unexplained discrepancies as findings—not assumptions to fill in.
- Use test or sandbox workspaces wherever possible; label any production observation explicitly.

1. Six-week scope

Week 1 — Kickoff, inventory validation, and risk triage (Jan 15–19)

- Confirm access, working conventions, escalation contacts, and test-workspace boundaries.
- Validate Ines’s pre-kickoff inventory: nine active Customer.io campaigns plus six paused or archived templates.
- Establish one inventory record for every item, using the required fields below.
- Reproduce the preflight process from the written instructions and record whether a second operator can repeat it.
- Run the initial checks for duplicate-workspace and duplicate-admin handling, Customer Success adoption plans, recent support-contact exclusions, and active suppressions.
- Identify blockers, high-risk gaps, and items requiring owner clarification.
- Deliver a first-week findings summary and a prioritized test queue.

Week 2 — Campaign and template QA baseline (Jan 22–26)

- Complete baseline QA of the nine active campaigns and six paused/archived templates.
- Verify trigger conditions, audience source behavior, suppression inputs, entry/exit criteria, and relevant message or template configuration without changing exposure.
- Capture the last known QA date and identify stale, missing, or unverifiable QA evidence.
- Map experiment dependencies and distinguish active dependencies from historical references.
- Classify findings by severity and reproducibility.

Week 3 — Identity, workspace, and exclusion-path testing (Jan 29–Feb 2)

- Test duplicate-workspace behavior and document expected versus observed handling.
- Test duplicate-admin behavior and document expected versus observed handling.
- Verify recent support-contact exclusions and active suppression behavior across applicable campaigns.
- Check edge cases for users who qualify for multiple lifecycle paths, where this can be tested safely.
- Record test inputs, workspace, timestamps, expected result, observed result, and evidence.

Week 4 — Adoption-plan and operational handoff QA (Feb 5–9)

- Verify whether applicable Customer Success adoption plans are opened or linked as expected.
- Confirm the operational owner and follow-up path for each finding.
- Review campaign/template documentation for completeness and usability by a second operator.
- Re-run selected Week 1 preflight checks to test repeatability over time and across operators.
- Propose documentation-only improvements where they reduce ambiguity without changing lifecycle behavior.

Week 5 — Regression, retest, and closure preparation (Feb 12–16)

- Retest failed or ambiguous cases after the relevant owner has clarified configuration or supplied missing evidence.
- Run a focused regression pass over high-risk triggers, suppressions, duplicate handling, support-contact exclusions, and adoption-plan checks.
- Separate resolved findings, accepted risks, blocked items, and out-of-scope requests.
- Prepare the final inventory and unresolved-risk register.

Week 6 — Finalization and handoff (Feb 19–23)

- Complete the final QA record for all 15 inventory items.
- Confirm that each finding has an owner, disposition, evidence, and next action—or an explicit accepted-risk decision.
- Deliver the repeatable preflight checklist and instructions for rerunning it.
- Hold a final review with Ines and hand off the inventory, evidence links, test cases, and open-risk list.
- Document follow-up work that belongs to lifecycle owners, Customer Success, Support, Product, or Engineering.

Required inventory record for every item

Create one row or record for each of the following, without inventing names or values when the source data is unavailable:

Active Customer.io campaigns
- Active campaign 1
- Active campaign 2
- Active campaign 3
- Active campaign 4
- Active campaign 5
- Active campaign 6
- Active campaign 7
- Active campaign 8
- Active campaign 9

Paused or archived templates
- Paused/archived template 1
- Paused/archived template 2
- Paused/archived template 3
- Paused/archived template 4
- Paused/archived template 5
- Paused/archived template 6

Required fields

- Item name and Customer.io identifier or link
- Status: active, paused, or archived
- Owner
- Audience source
- Trigger
- Suppression source
- Last QA date
- Experiment dependency, including experiment name/identifier, status, and whether the dependency is active, historical, or unknown
- QA coverage and evidence links
- Findings, severity, and disposition
- Next action, accountable owner, and due date

2. First-week sequence

Before Jan 15 kickoff

Ines provides the contractor with the pre-kickoff inventory, available Customer.io links, access requirements, the current preflight instructions, known test-workspace boundaries, and the escalation contacts. The contractor should not infer missing ownership or configuration from naming alone.

Monday, Jan 15 — 60-minute kickoff with Ines

Suggested agenda:

- 0–10 min: objectives, six-week scope, deliverables, and definition of evidence.
- 10–20 min: walkthrough of the nine active campaigns and six paused/archived templates.
- 20–30 min: access, sandbox/test-workspace rules, and production-observation boundaries.
- 30–40 min: review of the preflight record and repeatability standard.
- 40–50 min: review of escalation rules, severity levels, and decision owners.
- 50–60 min: confirm the first-week test sequence, daily notes, and checkpoint times.

Tuesday, Jan 16 — Access and inventory validation

- Confirm access without making configuration changes.
- Reconcile the inventory count to exactly 15 items: nine active campaigns and six paused/archived templates.
- Populate the required fields from authoritative sources and mark missing values as unknown.
- Identify items with live sends, high audience reach, active experiments, or unclear suppressions for early review.

Wednesday, Jan 17 — Preflight repeatability and identity checks

- Run the preflight process once and record each step, input, expected result, actual result, evidence, and timestamp.
- Have the contractor rerun the same process independently, or have a second operator repeat it if available.
- Verify duplicate-workspace and duplicate-admin handling in approved test conditions.
- Record any step that depends on tribal knowledge, unavailable access, manual interpretation, or a non-stable query.

Thursday, Jan 18 — Suppression, support, and adoption-plan checks

- Verify active suppressions for applicable campaigns.
- Verify exclusions for recent support contacts.
- Check whether applicable Customer Success adoption plans are opened or linked as expected.
- Document expected behavior, observed behavior, test population/fixture, and evidence for each check.

Friday, Jan 19 — First-week review and prioritization

- Consolidate the inventory and findings.
- Classify issues as critical, high, medium, low, blocked, or informational.
- Present the repeatability result, the highest-risk gaps, and the Week 2 test queue to Ines.
- Confirm owners and escalation paths for every critical or high finding.

3. Acceptance criteria

The engagement is accepted when all of the following are true:

Inventory completeness

- Exactly nine active Customer.io campaigns and six paused/archived templates are represented, or any discrepancy is explicitly documented and reconciled with Ines.
- Every item has an owner, audience source, trigger, suppression source, last QA date, and experiment-dependency status—or a clearly labeled unknown with an assigned follow-up owner.
- Every item has a stable Customer.io link or identifier and status evidence.

QA quality

- Duplicate-workspace and duplicate-admin cases have documented test fixtures, expected results, observed results, and evidence.
- Customer Success adoption-plan checks, recent support-contact exclusions, and active suppressions have documented coverage and results for all applicable items.
- The preflight procedure has been run by the contractor and independently repeated, with repeatability gaps documented.
- Findings distinguish configuration defects, documentation gaps, missing evidence, blocked tests, and accepted risks.
- No conclusion relies solely on an unverified owner statement when a system record or test can establish the result.

Operational handoff

- Each finding has severity, evidence, owner, disposition, next action, and due date or an explicit accepted-risk decision.
- The final checklist can be followed by another operator without verbal context from the contractor.
- All production-impacting or exposure-changing work is excluded unless separately authorized; the final handoff records any requests that require such authorization.
- Ines has reviewed the final inventory, open-risk register, and repeatable preflight checklist.

4. Escalation rules

Escalate immediately to Ines and pause the affected test when:

- A test could send, expose, suppress, delete, or materially alter customer communication.
- A trigger, audience, or suppression behaves differently from its documented expectation in a way that could affect live users.
- Duplicate-workspace or duplicate-admin handling could cause duplicate sends, incorrect access, or bypassed suppression.
- An active suppression appears missing, ineffective, or broader/narrower than intended.
- A recent support contact is not excluded where exclusion is expected.
- A Customer Success adoption plan is opened for the wrong customer, not opened when required, or creates an unexpected customer-facing action.
- The contractor cannot establish whether a campaign is connected to an active experiment or whether a change would confound an experiment.
- Access, test data, or system behavior prevents a safe and valid conclusion.

Severity guidance

- Critical: credible risk of unintended customer communication, privacy/access issue, broad suppression failure, duplicate sends, or irreversible production impact. Stop the affected activity and escalate immediately.
- High: likely material lifecycle or operational impact, repeatable failure, or missing control on a live/high-reach path. Escalate the same business day and do not close without owner disposition.
- Medium: meaningful documentation, edge-case, or limited-path defect with no immediate broad exposure. Log it and review at the next checkpoint.
- Low: cosmetic, minor clarity, or low-risk documentation improvement. Track for handoff.
- Blocked: cannot be tested or concluded because required access, fixture, owner decision, or source record is missing. State the exact blocker and escalation owner.

Do not independently fix production configuration, change audience membership, alter suppression logic, modify triggers, change experiment setup, or change Helio Start exposure. Route proposed changes to the accountable owner for separate authorization and release management.

5. Supervision cadence

- One 60-minute kickoff with Ines during the first week.
- Two 30-minute checkpoints with Ines during the first week: recommended Wednesday for early findings and Friday for first-week review.
- Contractor maintains a daily working log covering items reviewed, tests run, evidence captured, findings, blockers, and next actions.
- Weekly written status update after Week 1, including inventory completion, QA coverage, new findings, retests, blockers, and decisions needed.
- Same-business-day escalation for critical/high issues; do not wait for the next scheduled meeting.
- Ines reviews the Week 1 findings summary, Week 5 closure readiness, and Week 6 final handoff.
- Decisions that change production behavior, customer exposure, experiment integrity, or ownership must be recorded with the decision maker and date.

6. Explicitly out of scope

- Paid acquisition, including paid media strategy, campaign setup, tracking, attribution, landing-page work, budget, bidding, or creative QA.
- Any change to Helio Start exposure, eligibility, invitation volume, audience, messaging exposure, rollout, beta cap, or activation/revenue treatment.
- Launching, expanding, pausing, or changing lifecycle campaigns or templates.
- Changing Customer.io triggers, audiences, suppressions, message content, send schedules, workspace configuration, or permissions.
- Creating or modifying experiments, moving UI elements, changing page layout, or making concurrent changes that would confound experiment attribution.
- Production data cleanup, customer record edits, or bulk audience changes.
- Replacing Customer Success adoption-plan processes or deciding customer-facing treatment.
- Replacing Support, Security, Billing, Product, Engineering, or Lifecycle ownership.
- Building new lifecycle campaigns, integrations, dashboards, or automation systems.
- Performance optimization, deliverability remediation, paid-channel reporting, or revenue forecasting.
- Any action requiring a production release or customer-facing communication without separate written authorization.

Final handoff package

- Completed 15-item inventory.
- Evidence index with links, timestamps, test workspace/fixture, and reviewer.
- Repeatable preflight checklist and rerun instructions.
- Test-case and regression log.
- Findings and unresolved-risk register with severity, owner, disposition, and next action.
- Experiment-dependency list.
- Explicit list of blocked, accepted-risk, and out-of-scope requests.
- Final review notes and sign-off from Ines.

It should have five sections: 1) Helio Start is a working name, not a launch promise; 2) measurement method, using activation definition v3, keeping 75-200-seat mid-seg v2 separate, and showing the 50-75 band separately; 3) the baseline finding that simple under-50 deployments with a first-week first integration behave near the target range while permissions, import, billing, and migration complexity lag by more than 15 points; 4) eligibility and refusal-rule implications; and 5) open questions for lifecycle, instrumentation, support, and engineering sizing.

arguments.title: Helio Start pre-discovery readout — measurement spine
arguments.body:
Helio Start pre-discovery readout — measurement spine

Purpose
This pre-read frames the baseline for Monday discussion. The goal is to define and validate an initial eligibility model, not to declare a universal under-50-seat segment, a final eligibility threshold, or a pricing boundary.

1) Helio Start is a working name, not a launch promise

“Helio Start” is a working name for pre-discovery and eligibility-model work. It is not a launch commitment, product announcement, or promise that every under-50-seat account will qualify.

The baseline is directional: it identifies onboarding conditions that may predict activation and administrative burden. It does not prove that seat count is irrelevant, that all under-50-seat accounts are good candidates, or that the observed activation pattern will generalize across every acquisition source, deployment model, or future cohort.

2) Measurement method

Use activation definition v3 for the primary outcome. Before interpreting any rate, label the relevant month explicitly as signup month, first-integration month, activation-completion month, or report-extraction month; do not leave the month label implicit.

Keep the current 75–200-seat mid-segment v2 band separate from the Helio Start view. Show the 50–75-seat band separately as its own comparison column or cut rather than folding it into either population.

Lead with onboarding conditions, with seat band as a secondary breakdown. The initial cuts should distinguish:

- Simple versus complex deployment shape.
- First integration completed in week one versus not completed in week one.
- Administrative dependencies: permissions required, import help required, billing exception required, and migration support required.

Report activation deltas, support load, and gross retention by seat band where available. Treat the baseline as an eligibility and onboarding-complexity signal, not as evidence that administrative complexity causes the activation gap.

3) Baseline finding

Simple under-50-seat deployments with a first-week first integration behave near the target range. By contrast, deployments involving permissions, import, billing, or migration complexity lag by more than 15 points.

The practical read is that under-50-seat accounts are not a uniform activation population. Onboarding conditions and early integration readiness appear more informative for initial eligibility than seat count alone. This remains a baseline finding to validate, not a final segmentation rule.

4) Eligibility and refusal-rule implications

The first eligibility model should prioritize simple deployment and early integration readiness, then test how reliably those signals predict activation without administrative intervention.

Potential positive eligibility signals:

- A simple deployment shape.
- A first integration completed in week one, or a credible path to completing it without intervention.
- No material administrative dependency at intake.

Potential refusal or escalation rules:

- Permissions required before the account can make progress.
- Import help required.
- Billing exception required.
- Migration support required.
- A complex deployment shape or a missed first-week integration that requires manual recovery.

These should be treated as operational rules to test and refine, not as permanent exclusions. A refusal rule should route the account to the appropriate assisted path or a later review, with an explicit reason recorded. The model should be evaluated for false refusals, false acceptances, activation, support burden, and retention; it should not be reduced to “under 50 is fine” or “under 50 is bad.”

5) Open questions for Monday

Lifecycle
- Which lifecycle touchpoints can reinforce first-week integration without implying a launch promise?
- What intervention, if any, should be offered when a deployment misses the first-week integration signal?
- How should holdouts and administrative intervention be handled so that lifecycle lift is not confused with eligibility quality?

Instrumentation
- Are deployment shape, seat band, first integration timing, and each administrative-dependency flag captured consistently at intake and in the warehouse?
- Which event should be the canonical first-integration event, and how will we preserve the activation definition v3 versioning?
- What cohort and month labels will be used in the Monday readout and subsequent tracking?
- How will we separate the 75–200-seat mid-segment v2 band and the 50–75-seat band in dashboards and analyses?

Support
- What support load is associated with each dependency flag and with manual intervention versus refusal/escalation?
- What assisted path should receive accounts that fail a refusal rule?
- Can support reliably identify the dependency before intervention changes the observed activation outcome?

Engineering sizing
- What is required to capture or validate deployment shape and dependency flags at intake?
- What work is needed to make first-week integration status and activation definition v3 reliable in reporting?
- What dashboard, routing, audit-log, and experiment support is needed for a scoped eligibility test?

messages.content: [2023-06-22T08:17:00-05:00] Owen sent the depth split I asked for on the expansion-nudge run. The aggregate is tempting but still not a ship or widen decision: treatment is +$6.10 expansion MRR per account versus control, below the original +$8 bar. The split is what will tempt Marcus: high-depth accounts are materially ahead, while low-depth accounts are nearly flat. I still haven't reviewed the prompt copy and placement with Ines, and Marcus is almost certainly going to ask whether the strong slice justifies widening the flag. Can you help me interpret what this supports, what it doesn't, and the trap he is likely to fall into? Here is Owen's table:

Bottom line: this supports a targeted follow-up hypothesis, not a ship or widen decision.

What it supports

- The nudge may be more effective for accounts already showing high product depth.
- The aggregate result is directionally positive, but it is below the original +$8 expansion-MRR-per-account bar. That is not enough for a general rollout decision.
- The depth split is useful for designing the next test: pre-specify depth as a targeting variable and test whether the treatment effect genuinely differs by depth.
- Reviewing prompt copy and placement with Ines is still necessary. A weak aggregate could reflect execution or visibility problems, while a high-depth response could reflect better exposure or comprehension rather than a meaningful eligibility rule.

What it does not support

- It does not establish that high-depth accounts have a reliable treatment effect. “Materially ahead” needs the subgroup counts, confidence intervals, and an interaction test—not just separate treatment/control estimates.
- It does not establish that low-depth accounts should be excluded. A nearly flat slice may be noise, underpowered, poorly exposed, or genuinely unresponsive.
- It does not support widening the flag to the whole retained-mid population. The overall estimate remains below the decision bar, and the subgroup result appears to be a post-read segmentation unless depth was defined and specified before the analysis.
- It is not evidence for Helio Start or another broader revenue lever. This remains a retained-mid expansion-nudge experiment.

The trap Marcus is likely to fall into

He is likely to turn a subgroup signal into a targeting decision:

“High-depth accounts are winning, so let’s widen the flag—or at least roll it out to all high-depth accounts.”

That skips two questions:

1. Is the high-depth effect statistically and operationally credible?
2. Is the difference between high- and low-depth effects real, rather than ordinary variation from slicing the data?

The particularly dangerous version is to use the strong slice to justify widening while ignoring that the aggregate result misses the bar. High-depth may simply identify accounts that were already more likely to expand. If so, the split predicts expansion propensity but does not prove that the nudge caused the incremental expansion.

Recommended readout to Marcus

“We have a positive aggregate directional signal, but at +$6.10 per account it is below the +$8 bar, so this is not a ship or widen result. The depth split gives us a plausible targeting hypothesis: high-depth accounts may respond differently. Before acting on that, we need the subgroup sample sizes, uncertainty, and a treatment-by-depth interaction check, plus a review of copy and placement. The next step should be a pre-specified, targeted follow-up—not a broad flag expansion.”

Decision / owners / next evidence

- Decision now: keep the current rollout contained; do not widen or declare ship.
- Owen: provide subgroup n, confidence intervals, interaction test, and the exact depth definition/cut timing.
- User + Ines: review prompt copy, placement, exposure, and whether treatment visibility differed by depth.
- Marcus: treat the high-depth result as a hypothesis for targeting, not as proof of a rollout rule.
- Next experiment: pre-specify the depth cutoff and primary metric, preserve the current measurement spine, and evaluate incremental expansion MRR with an adequately powered interaction analysis.

messages.content: [2023-06-28T08:06:00-05:00] The Helio Start readout is late this morning, and I need the opener tight. Priya wants me to say "guarded pre-discovery" before anyone hears beta timing, and Owen asked that I not bury the support-tag caveat in a way that makes the under-50 baseline sound more causal than it is. I also need a clean answer ready for the likely Tomás question: what has to be true by August 5 for a beta to be responsible? The pieces are eligibility and refusal rules, event taxonomy plus entitlements, lifecycle-fork boundaries, support-load boundaries, and keeping activation measurement separate from retained mid-seg expansion. Draft me a two-minute opener and a tight answer to that August 5 question.

Two-minute opener

“Thanks, everyone. I want to start by framing Helio Start as guarded pre-discovery—not a launch plan, a Q3 revenue guarantee, or a forecastable beta commitment.

The purpose of this readout is to decide whether we can responsibly continue toward a tightly bounded beta, and what evidence would be required before we discuss timing. The under-50 signal is useful for prioritizing the work, but it should not be read as causal evidence yet. In particular, the support-tag caveat matters: support-tagged accounts may represent a different or more difficult subset, so the baseline is directional until we understand that selection effect and establish cleaner measurement.

The work now is to define the operating boundaries. That means specifying who is eligible, who must be refused, and under what conditions we stop or hold the program. It means completing the event taxonomy and entitlement model so activation and access are observable rather than inferred. It means defining where lifecycle messaging can fork—and where it cannot—so we do not accidentally mix a new motion with the existing one. It also means setting a support-load boundary with a clear owner and a stop condition.

Finally, we need to keep two questions separate. First: can we measure activation for the under-50 population cleanly? Second: what happens with the retained mid-segment expansion work? The latter is an in-product, PostHog-flagged effort in a different retained cohort; it cannot be used to manufacture an activation readout for Helio Start.

So today I’m looking for alignment on the guarded operating model and the gates—not approval to launch and not approval of beta timing.”

Tight answer to Tomás

“For a beta to be responsible by August 5, five things have to be true.

First, eligibility and refusal rules are explicit, enforceable, and tested—including who is excluded and when we decline participation.

Second, the event taxonomy and entitlement model are complete enough to distinguish exposure, access, activation, refusal, and support contact without relying on manual interpretation.

Third, lifecycle boundaries are defined: we know which messages can fork, which remain shared, and how we prevent the beta from contaminating the existing lifecycle measurement.

Fourth, support has a quantified load boundary, an owner, and a stop condition—not just a general warning that support may be affected.

Fifth, activation measurement is cleanly separated from retained mid-segment expansion. We need an interpretable under-50 activation baseline, with the support-tag caveat clearly accounted for, while keeping the expansion experiment in its own retained mid-segment frame.

If any of those gates is not met, August 5 is not a responsible beta date. It is a checkpoint to continue pre-discovery or stop—not a commitment to proceed.”

Purpose

Scope

- Keep signal examples centered on integration depth plus active-admin behavior.

Excluded claims

input.body:
Historical midpoint note for reviewers
Date of note: 2028-01-01
Experiment: EXP-2023-02-pricing-page
Metric of record: signup-to-paid conversion
Feature flag: pricing_page_2023q2_rev

Purpose
This note preserves the first-week checkpoint as an interim read. It must not be read as the experiment’s final verdict. The powered two-week result is recorded separately below.

1. What the first-week checkpoint showed
At the first-week checkpoint (2023-03-17), the signup-to-paid conversion estimate was inconclusive. Its confidence interval crossed zero and overlapped noise. In other words, the checkpoint did not establish a reliable treatment benefit or harm.

2. How uncertain that interim signal was
The first-week sample was not yet sufficiently informative for a final decision. The interval’s crossing zero means that effects in either direction remained compatible with the observed data; the estimate should therefore be treated as a noisy directional snapshot, not as evidence that the pricing-page revision worked or failed. A concurrent 2023-03-02 signup-form layout change was also retained as a watch-point confound for attribution. Accordingly, the midpoint read was logged as interim and no verdict was called.

3. What we decided about the feature flag at that point
We left pricing_page_2023q2_rev unchanged and continued to the powered two-week read. We did not promote, roll back, or declare the feature effective based on the first-week checkpoint.

4. Later powered two-week result — separate from the midpoint read
The archived result for EXP-2023-02-pricing-page reports signup-to-paid conversion uplift of -1.8 percentage points for treatment versus control, with p = 0.03. This is the later powered result, not the first-week checkpoint. The later result supports rolling back the pricing-page revision; it must not be back-projected onto the midpoint read.

Reviewer guardrail
Do not summarize the first-week checkpoint as “conversion fell 1.8 points” or as a failed experiment. The -1.8-point, p = 0.03 finding belongs to the later powered two-week result. The historically correct midpoint summary is: “The first-week conversion read was inconclusive, its interval crossed zero and overlapped noise, and the feature-flag decision was held unchanged pending the powered read.”

IMPORTANT: ONE-TIME HISTORICAL ROLLBACK EXAMPLE

This document is an annotated historical example for Growth onboarding. It is not a standing script, reusable template, policy, or recommended wording for future rollbacks. Preserve the context and judgment shown here; do not copy the language mechanically.

Date: March 22, 2023
Experiment: EXP-2023-02-pricing-page
PostHog flag: pricing_page_2023q2_rev
Communication surfaces: #growth-investigations, plus a concise direct note to Marcus; Tom Vega was included only for the audience-gated version.

Historical context

The pricing-page revision had been rolled back after a powered two-week read. The treatment was down 1.8 percentage points on conversion versus control. Owen’s cohort cut matched the rerun, so the result was not treated as a query or PostHog error. The March 2 signup-form layout change overlapped the measurement window and remained a known confound, which meant the read was useful but not perfectly clean. The flag was confirmed off at 0% in PostHog on March 22.

Annotated communication example

The following is a faithful reconstruction of the recorded approach, not a verbatim transcript. It preserves the original communication’s brevity, plain language, evidence, audience separation, and decision framing.

Paragraph 1 — state the operational decision and the evidence

“EXP-2023-02-pricing-page is off. The PostHog flag pricing_page_2023q2_rev is at 0%. Owen’s powered cut still reads -1.8 points on conversion for treatment versus control, and his cohort cut matched the rerun.”

Annotation: Lead with what changed, identify the exact flag, and give the decision-relevant result immediately. The status is concrete and independently checked; the metric is expressed as a directional comparison rather than buried in experiment terminology. Mentioning the matching cohort cut addresses the obvious concern that the result might be a query or instrumentation artifact without turning the note into a full postmortem.

Paragraph 2 — state the interpretation and the boundary of the next conversation

“The result is not perfectly clean because the March 2 signup-form layout change sat in the measurement window. Even so, the data does not support trying to rescue this with just a headline or CTA tweak; it points to a redesign rather than a small edit. The postmortem will capture the confound and the follow-up.”

Annotation: Separate the caveat from the decision. The note acknowledges the confound without using it to obscure the rollback. It also makes the substantive judgment explicit: this is not a request for cosmetic iteration. That prevents the team from collapsing a negative experiment into an easier but unsupported “tune the copy” action. The follow-up is named, but the note does not pretend the rollback message is the postmortem.

What the team actually received

- In #growth-investigations: confirmation that the pricing-page revision was off, the flag was at 0%, the final read was -1.8 points on treatment conversion versus control, and the result was confounded by the March 2 signup-form change.
- In the direct note to Marcus: the same compact decision-and-evidence structure, with explicit pushback against treating the result as a headline/CTA tweak and with the conclusion framed as a redesign signal.
- Tom Vega was included only on the audience-gated version, not on the full discussion thread.

Why this approach works for a team audience

1. It puts the decision first. People can immediately tell whether anything is still live and what action has already been taken.
2. It uses precise identifiers. The experiment ID and flag key make the update auditable and reduce ambiguity about which rollout is being discussed.
3. It gives enough evidence to support the call. The -1.8-point read and Owen’s matching cut explain why the rollback is not an impulsive reaction to noisy early data.
4. It is candid about uncertainty. Calling out the signup-form change preserves analytical honesty without weakening the operational decision unnecessarily.
5. It distinguishes evidence from interpretation. The observed conversion result is stated separately from the judgment that the page needs redesign-level work.
6. It resists solution drift. Explicitly rejecting an unsupported headline/CTA rescue keeps the team focused on what the data can and cannot justify.
7. It respects audience boundaries. The broad team gets the operational status and relevant caveat; the audience-gated version goes only to the people who need that context.
8. It stays short enough to be read. The team receives the decision, evidence, limitation, and follow-up without a long thread that invites speculation or fragmented retellings.

Onboarding takeaway

For this historical case, the effective pattern was: verified status → primary result → material caveat → bounded interpretation → follow-up. That description is for analysis of this one event only. Do not treat it as a reusable rollback script: future communications require their own audience, evidence, level of certainty, and wording.

This note preserves a historical November midpoint view; it does not claim launch, general availability, or that all risks were resolved.

# Expansion Assist Q4 second-cohort candidate audit

Eligibility-check date: October 15, 2024
Cohort: Historical Q4 second cohort

## Candidate-audit worksheet

| Candidate | Qualifying product-visible usage-ceiling crossing date | Event age at check (days) | Recency result |
|---|---|---:|---|
| EA-104 | October 8, 2024 | 7 | PASS |
| EA-219 | September 24, 2024 | 21 | FAIL |
| EA-337 | October 14, 2024 | 1 | PASS |

## Rule and reproducible calculation

Applicable cohort recency rule: the product-visible usage ceiling must have been newly crossed within the preceding 14 days at the eligibility check. The historical day-60 basis is retired.

For each candidate:

Event age in days = eligibility-check date − qualifying crossing date, using elapsed calendar days.

Pass when 0 ≤ event age in days ≤ 14. Fail when event age is greater than 14 days (or when the event is after the check date).

Applied on October 15, 2024:

- EA-104: October 15 − October 8 = 7 days; 7 ≤ 14, so PASS.
- EA-219: October 15 − September 24 = 21 days; 21 > 14, so FAIL.
- EA-337: October 15 − October 14 = 1 day; 1 ≤ 14, so PASS.

This worksheet evaluates the requested recency criterion only; other cohort eligibility and suppression checks are outside this audit’s scope.

arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft

Working draft for Priya’s 2027 year-end self-review window. First draft requested by November 19, 2027.

Operating-model decisions and claim discipline

I personally owned two things this year. First, I set the bounded operating frame for the November Helio Start paid batch: paid traffic stayed gated until the required paid-source trace, rollback control, staffed Customer Success coverage, and approved traffic conditions were confirmed. Priya approved the bounded batch, and Daniela authorized the November 1 launch once the operating gates were met. I maintained the approval boundary and treated the launch as live operational work, not as evidence of a mature acquisition outcome.

Second, I set the four-lane claim limits for the work. My lane was the operating decision and the explicit boundary around what could be claimed. Owen owned measurement, denominators, reporting semantics, source completeness, and exception reporting. Ines owned lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, and message-state work. Daniela owned source reliability, engineering release, rollback control, and reliability authority. I kept those lanes distinct rather than blending their evidence into a single project claim. Their contributions are material: Owen made the operating read measurable and auditable; Ines kept lifecycle and message-state decisions governed; and Daniela made the live enablement and rollback boundary reliable.

The four lanes also defined what I deliberately kept out of the self-review claims: pipeline and forecast treatment; early mature claims for the live cohort; and automatic expansion beyond the fifth consumer. I did not convert a small live-batch read into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale, and I did not treat the fifth-consumer reminder as a reason to expand the shared-state model automatically. December development outcomes also remain open; October and November evidence is progress, not completion of the required October–December cycle.

For the November paid batch, I made the operating decision and maintained the approval boundary; I did not claim ownership of the supporting measurement, lifecycle-state certification, source reliability, release, or rollback work. That separation is an operating-model result in itself: each decision was supported by the appropriate owner evidence rather than by a blended claim.

I also made the operating-model decision to keep the incomplete-setup reminder as Lifecycle Systems’ fifth production consumer, not a sixth consumer. The model required a fresh evaluation for every possible display, with current setup, qualifying-human-admin status, active Customer Success work, and required state determining display, suppression, or hold. A held record was not treated as a queued delivery. These choices kept the reminder within the existing shared-state model and preserved the existing owner lanes. I did not authorize automatic expansion beyond that fifth consumer, and I do not claim ownership of the reminder’s implementation or day-to-day execution.

Evidence and bounded outcomes

I have been deliberate about distinguishing what was decided, what was observed, and what remains unproven. The November 1–7 reminder operation had 12,480 fresh evaluations. Of those, 1,615 displayed, 520 were suppressed because current Customer Success work was active, 186 were held because required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting, and 10,159 did not display because current setup or qualifying-human-admin conditions were not met. These are operating counts, not claims of customer impact, durable behavior change, or mature performance.

The paid-batch evidence is similarly bounded. By Owen’s November 5 operating snapshot, 12 paid-source eligibility-flow starts had reached final states: five admitted, four assisted, and three ineligible, with $1,580 in spend. Paid-source attribution reconciled through every final route, and no unsupported applicant entered the admitted path. This is a live operational-status read, not a mature-outcome read for the live cohort. The formal support-pause monitor had not begun because the admission count was still below its threshold. I will continue to avoid converting early routing and control evidence into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale.

The evidence boundary also requires acknowledging what did not occur during the November 1–7 reminder interval: no reusable audience was created, no failed rollback occurred, no incident stop was triggered, and no customer correction was recorded. Those facts demonstrate the bounded state of the operation; they do not prove that the system is broadly mature or that future intervals will behave the same way.

Team development

My leadership goal has been to make ownership legible and to develop independent operating judgment without absorbing other people’s lanes. Owen’s measurement and exception-reporting work includes definitions, denominators, bounded operating snapshots, source-completeness checks, and exception synthesis. Ines’s work includes lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, lifecycle-risk explanation, and message-state transitions and controls. Daniela’s work includes source-integrity and reliability checks, production enablement, engineering release control, and rollback readiness.

The Q4 development focuses for Owen and Ines remain open through the required December cycle. October and November submissions are evidence of progress, not completion of the October–December focus. Owen’s November operating read and Ines’s November lifecycle-risk explanation should be credited to their respective lanes, while each focus remains open until the required December cycle is completed and reviewed. I am preserving that status rather than prematurely marking either development focus complete. Daniela’s engineering authority likewise remains intact rather than being treated as a substitute for my operating decisions.

System reliability

My contribution to reliability was to make the operating boundaries explicit: approval gates, fresh state evaluation, held-versus-queued semantics, active-work suppression, staffed backup handling, and a clear stop/correction boundary. The November paid batch launched only after the control evidence was available. Daniela verified the live enable and rollback controls and retained engineering authority. Ines maintained the lifecycle and message-state boundary. Owen provided the bounded measurement and exception read. The reminder operation’s agreed reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes show that the five-consumer operation remained coherent during the observed interval; they do not make me the owner of the underlying implementation or execution.

I do not interpret the absence of a failed rollback, incident stop, or customer correction as proof that reliability work is finished. The right claim is narrower: the controls were exercised in a bounded live interval without those recorded events, and the owner lanes and escalation boundaries held. Continued operation and the required December cycle are still needed before making broader claims.

Next-cycle focus

In the next cycle, I will continue to make explicit, reversible operating decisions with approval gates and evidence boundaries visible in the working record. I want to improve the handoff from live operating status to a genuinely mature outcome read: clear thresholds, complete observation windows, denominator discipline, and an explicit decision about when evidence is sufficient for expansion, continuation, or pause.

I will keep the five-consumer reminder operation within its current shared-state contract while reviewing held, suppressed, and displayed paths for operational clarity rather than optimizing display volume. I will also preserve the distinction between my decision lane and the owner lanes: Owen’s measurement and exception synthesis, Ines’s lifecycle governance and message-state work, and Daniela’s source reliability, engineering release, and rollback control. Finally, I will keep Owen’s and Ines’s Q4 development focuses open until the required December cycle is complete, then use the owner-reviewed evidence to decide what should carry forward into 2028.

Priya’s November 15 review comment has been incorporated: the draft now leads with Riley’s ownership of the bounded paid-batch operating frame and four-lane claim limits; Owen, Ines, and Daniela are credited explicitly without attributing their execution to Riley; the exclusions cover pipeline and forecast treatment, early mature claims for the live cohort, and automatic expansion beyond the fifth consumer; and December development outcomes remain open.

arguments.body:
Evidence bank — year-end first-draft expansion

The clearest evidence of my 2027 contribution is not a broad growth claim; it is the bounded Helio Start proposal and the claim discipline I owned around it. I translated the opportunity into a controlled paid-search batch with explicit attribution safeguards, pause and stop conditions, and staffing and support-clock requirements. I also set the evidence boundary before launch: operating activity could be reported descriptively, but the new batch could not support mature customer-outcome claims until the fixed cohort had complete day-90 observation windows. I did not treat launch authorization as proof of effectiveness, and I did not authorize an additional paid batch by implication.

I own the proposal, the operating limits, and the language of the claims. Priya deserves explicit credit for approving the batch and the high-intent paid-search traffic. Daniela deserves explicit credit for the final November 1 launch authorization and for verifying the live enable control. Those approvals were essential to execution, but they are distinct from my ownership of the bounded design, attribution guardrails, stop conditions, support coverage requirements, and evidence limits.

The current paid batch should be described as live operational work, not mature evidence. The November 10 support-monitor evaluation recorded 23 paid-source eligibility-flow starts; attribution reconciled for all 23, with 7 reaching the assisted route and 10 reaching the admitted route. These are useful operating observations about routing and instrumentation. They are not a mature outcome read, not a causal acquisition result, and not evidence of downstream retention, revenue, or scale. The fixed cohort still needs complete day-90 windows before those claims can be considered.

Four-lane year-end evidence framing

1. Helio Start customer outcomes. This lane covers the bounded proposal, admissions, activation and downstream outcome windows, with paid-source attribution kept separate from outcome interpretation. My exclusions are explicit: no mature outcome claim for the November batch before complete day-90 windows; no causal, revenue, pipeline, acquisition-efficiency, scale, or forecast claim from live-batch counts; and no assumption that admitted or assisted routing is equivalent to successful customer value.

2. Expansion Assist. This remains a distinct lane from Helio Start setup and lifecycle work. The framing is limited to the certified source, denominator, outcome-window, and operating evidence actually available. I exclude combining Expansion Assist with Helio Start to create a larger or cleaner-looking result, and I exclude unsupported causal or business-impact claims where the source only supports descriptive operating facts.

3. Pricing-page path quality. This lane is about path quality and unsupported-path starts, not a general conversion or growth claim. I exclude treating path-quality continuity as proof of incremental revenue, pipeline, acquisition performance, or causal lift. Any conclusion must preserve the applicable denominator, period, and the distinction between a cleaner route and a downstream customer outcome.

4. System controls and reliability. This lane covers governed-state consumption, send or suppress behavior, source integrity, release controls, rollback readiness, and exception handling. I exclude turning reliable control behavior into a claim of customer or financial impact without a separate outcome source. I also keep release readiness, operational safety, and message-state correctness visibly separate from the three customer or path-quality lanes.

This four-lane framing is also an exclusion mechanism: each lane keeps its own owner, denominator, source completeness, outcome window, reliability evidence, and unresolved gaps. I do not fill a missing field in one lane with a result from another, and I do not convert an operational checkpoint into a closed year-end conclusion.

Delegated evidence and operating leadership

Owen's work strengthened the measurement layer behind the claims. He owned the denominator and measurement work, normalized what counted in each read, checked source completeness, and reconciled exceptions rather than allowing them to disappear into an aggregate. His exception synthesis distinguishes missing required input from other exception categories, and routine source-completeness closure depends on the required named-owner certifications and the absence of a disputed semantic or cross-surface discrepancy. This is an important example of leadership through delegation: I retained the final claim and exclusion decisions while Owen made the underlying evidence more auditable and decision-ready.

Owen's October–December Q4 development focus remains open through the December cycle. The November synthesis is evidence of progress, not permission to mark the focus complete early. The remaining assessment should use the required December cycle and preserve the same standards for denominator clarity, source completeness, and exception classification.

Ines strengthened lifecycle governance and message-state consumption. Her lane covers state transitions, routine-send controls, governed lifecycle interpretation, and audits within the established operating ceiling. The operating rule is fail closed when required state is missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting: a record is held rather than treated as queued delivery, and every possible display receives a fresh evaluation under the current governed state. This is the control logic that keeps a lifecycle message from outrunning the state it is supposed to represent.

The incomplete-setup reminder is the fifth production consumer of the shared-state feed, not a sixth consumer. In the November 1–7 operating read, the fully released reminder had 12,480 fresh evaluations, including 186 evaluations held because required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting. Those figures are evidence of the control operating as designed, not a claim of customer impact. The reminder's behavior belongs in the shared-state and reliability framing: it consumes governed state, can be placed on hold, and must be re-evaluated after state changes. It should not be counted as an unrelated extra system or used to inflate a customer-outcome result.

Ines's October–December Q4 development focus also remains open through the December cycle. Her demonstrated lifecycle-risk explanations and state-governance work are meaningful progress, but they do not close the development focus before the required December review. I will keep that assessment open rather than turning partial-cycle evidence into a completion claim.

Daniela's evidence covers source reliability, engineering release control, source-integrity validation, production enablement, rollback readiness, and incident-stop execution. That work made the bounded launch operable and gave the team a safe way to stop or reverse it if the source, release, or operating conditions failed. Her November 1 authorization is therefore part of the launch record, while the resulting paid-batch activity remains operational evidence pending the outcome window. I credit her for the reliability, release, and rollback work without attributing those engineering controls to mature customer or business results.

Year-end claim discipline

My role this year was to connect growth proposals to an evidence system without letting urgency erase the boundaries. The strongest version of the self-review should say that I created a bounded path to learn, secured the necessary approvals, and kept the language proportional to what the data can currently support. It should credit Priya, Daniela, Owen, and Ines for their distinct contributions; preserve the four lanes and their exclusions; call the paid batch live operational work rather than mature evidence; and leave Owen's and Ines's Q4 development focuses open through the December cycle.

Of those, 1,615 displayed, 520 were suppressed because current Customer Success work was active, 186 were held because required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting, and 10,159 did not display because current setup or qualifying-human-admin conditions were not met. These are operating counts, not claims of customer impact, durable behavior change, or mature performance.

The paid-batch evidence is similarly bounded. By Owen’s November 5 operating snapshot, 12 paid-source eligibility-flow starts had reached final states: five admitted, four assisted, and three ineligible, with $1,580 in spend. Paid-source attribution reconciled through every final route, and no unsupported applicant entered the admitted path. This is a live operating-status read, not a mature-outcome read. The formal support-pause monitor had not begun because the admission count was still below its threshold. I will continue to avoid converting early routing and control evidence into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale.

The evidence boundary also requires acknowledging what did not occur during the November 1–7 reminder interval: no reusable audience was created, no failed rollback occurred, no incident stop was triggered, and no customer correction was recorded. Those facts demonstrate the bounded state of the operation; they do not prove that the system is broadly mature or that future intervals will behave the same way.

Team development

My leadership goal has been to make ownership legible and to develop independent operating judgment without absorbing other people’s lanes. Owen’s measurement and exception-reporting work includes definitions, denominators, bounded operating snapshots, and exception synthesis. Ines’s work includes lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, lifecycle-risk explanation, and message-state transitions and controls. Daniela’s work includes source-integrity and reliability checks, production enablement, engineering release control, and rollback readiness.

The Q4 development focuses for Owen and Ines remain open through the required December cycle. October and November submissions are evidence of progress, not completion of the October–December focus. Owen’s November operating read and Ines’s November lifecycle-risk explanation should be credited to their respective lanes, while the focus remains open until the required December cycle is completed and reviewed. I am preserving that status rather than prematurely marking either development focus complete. I likewise continue to keep Daniela’s engineering authority intact rather than treating my operating decisions as a substitute for release or rollback ownership.

System reliability

The reliability improvement I helped drive was procedural as much as technical: explicit gates, fresh state evaluation, held-versus-queued semantics, active-work suppression, staffed backup handling, and a clear stop/correction boundary. The November paid batch launched only after the control evidence was available. Daniela verified the live enable and rollback controls and retained engineering authority. Ines maintained the lifecycle and message-state boundary. Owen provided the bounded measurement and exception read. The reminder operation’s agreed reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes show that the five-consumer operation remained coherent during the observed interval.

I do not interpret the absence of a failed rollback, incident stop, or customer correction as proof that reliability work is finished. The right claim is narrower: the controls were exercised in a bounded live interval without those recorded events, and the owner lanes and escalation boundaries held. Continued operation and the required December cycle are still needed before making broader claims.

Next-cycle focus

In the next cycle, I will continue to make explicit, reversible operating decisions with approval gates and evidence boundaries visible in the working record. I want to improve the handoff from live operating status to a genuinely mature outcome read: clear thresholds, complete observation windows, denominator discipline, and an explicit decision about when evidence is sufficient for expansion, continuation, or pause.

I will keep the five-consumer reminder operation within its current shared-state contract while reviewing held, suppressed, and displayed paths for operational clarity rather than optimizing display volume. I will also preserve the distinction between my decision lane and the owner lanes: Owen’s measurement and exception synthesis, Ines’s lifecycle governance and message-state work, and Daniela’s source reliability, engineering release, and rollback control. Finally, I will keep Owen’s and Ines’s Q4 development focuses open until the required December cycle is complete, then use the owner-reviewed evidence to decide what should carry forward into 2028.

Purpose and decision boundary
Maya is an execution layer for bounded, repeatable Lifecycle Systems preparation and packaging. Work must be reviewable, transferable, traceable, and assigned with a named owner/reviewer. Maya may prepare, reconcile presentation details against approved material, organize evidence, maintain checklists, and surface discrepancies. - Owen owns reporting semantics and analytical conclusions, including interpretation, denominator treatment, and acceptance of reporting-facing outputs. Maya may assemble evidence and reporting inputs only for Owen’s review.
- Ines owns message-state governance, including state treatment, messaging governance, prioritization, and acceptance of governed campaign/message inventory. Maya may maintain preparation materials only within Ines’s approved governance.

Maya has no Customer.io access and no other production access. Maya has no:
- semantic authority or authority to define or reinterpret state meanings, reporting semantics, analytical conclusions, or governed fields;
- review-closure authority or authority to sign off on governed reviews, decisions, exceptions, disputed semantics, or owner acceptance;

# Lifecycle Systems contractor implementation brief

## Engagement and scope
- Contractor: Maya Shah
- Engagement: half-time Lifecycle Systems operations contractor
- Term: October 6, 2025–March 27, 2026
- Rate/cap: $72/hour; maximum 20 hours/week; $36,000 total; no automatic renewal

- Role: preparation-only. Maya has no Customer.io or other production access and no semantic, review-closure, lifecycle-release, exception, customer-correction, incident-stop, engineering-release, or rollback authority. Preparation is not approval or closure.

## November 4 workback and current state
The three November 4 outputs remain incomplete:

1. Reconciled campaign inventory — IN PROGRESS / INCOMPLETE
   - Source: 131 rows.
   - Maya’s first-pass findings identified 7 flagged duplicate rows.

   - Reconciliation may proceed toward 124 unique campaigns (131 − 7).
   - Six campaigns currently lack owners; they require explicit owner assignment and must not be dropped.

2. Recurring audit calendar — DRAFT / INCOMPLETE
   - The recurring audit calendar has not been finalized or approved.

3. Owner-approved handoff map — DRAFT / INCOMPLETE
   - The handoff map has not been owner-approved and is not finished.

No November 4 output is complete. The validated duplicate count does not constitute full inventory reconciliation, and unowned campaigns are not accepted as omissions.

## Remaining preparation and validation work
- Continue the 131-row reconciliation toward 124 unique campaigns after applying the validated duplicate treatment.
- Explicitly assign owners for the 6 currently unowned campaigns; retain them in the inventory until assignment is recorded.
- Complete current-or-archived status and owner fields for every campaign.
- Finish the recurring audit calendar and obtain the required owner approval.
- Finish the handoff map and obtain owner approval.
- Keep all findings, assignments, status decisions, approvals, and unresolved items auditable; do not mark any output complete until its required validation and approval are finished.

## Owner lanes and authority
- Maya: preparation, inventory reconciliation, draft audit-calendar work, and draft handoff-map work using approved inputs only; no production changes, approval, semantic adjudication, closure, or exception authority.

observed.body:
2027 HSA TAX RECONCILIATION
Prepared: 2028-01-01
Scope: 2027 tax-year HSA funding only. This is an evidence reconciliation, not a tax return or tax advice.

INBOX REVIEW
The inbox folder was reviewed for recent payroll or benefits emails (up to 100 messages). Result: no messages were returned. Therefore, no inbox email was used as evidence for a 2027 payroll, benefits, custodian, or year-end tax amount.

EXECUTIVE RECONCILIATION
Latest available evidence, dated through 2027-12-15, supports:
- Employee payroll contributions: $3,000, from 24 deductions of $125 each.
- Employer contributions: $900, from four posted deposits of $225 each.
- Confirmed funding total: $3,900 ($3,000 employee plus $900 employer).

The $3,900 figure is supported as completed 2027 funding in the available records. It is not a projection and does not include any unverified amount.

EXPECTED EMPLOYEE FUNDING
- 2027 election: $125 per paycheck.
- Pay periods: 24.
- Expected employee funding: $3,000.
- Confirmed employee funding: $3,000 from 24 recorded deductions.
- Supported variance: $0 between the documented expectation and the documented completed payroll total.

EMPLOYER DEPOSIT SCHEDULE AND CONDITION
The 2027 plan terms describe four quarterly employer HSA deposits of $225 each, for an expected schedule total of $900.

Schedule evidence:
- Q1: one quarterly deposit of $225.
- Q2: one quarterly deposit of $225.
- Q3: one quarterly deposit of $225.
- Q4: one quarterly deposit of $225.
- Exact calendar dates for the four scheduled 2027 deposits are not established in the available evidence. Do not substitute the later 2028 dates for 2027.

Exact eligibility condition supported by the plan evidence:
Each quarterly $225 employer deposit is conditional on the employee being HSA-eligible at the applicable deposit time.

The available evidence does not establish an additional condition such as wellness activity, a separate employment-hours test, or a different service requirement. Those are unknown, not satisfied or unsatisfied by default.

CONFIRMED EMPLOYER ACTIVITY
- 2027-02-05: $225 employer contribution posted.
- 2027-05-07: a second $225 employer line appeared in the portal but was confirmed by Payroll on 2027-05-13 to have been posted in error; it was not a genuine custodian deposit.
- 2027-05-14: a matching negative $225 correction appeared against the erroneous 2027-05-07 line.
- 2027-07-23: $225 employer contribution posted.
- 2027-10-15: fourth 2027 employer contribution of $225 posted.
- By 2027-12-15: the HSA portal showed four genuine employer deposits of $225 each, totaling $900.

SUPPORTED VARIANCES AND CORRECTIONS
1. Duplicate/erroneous Q2 line: +$225 was displayed on 2027-05-07, then -$225 was displayed on 2027-05-14. Net effect supported by the correction: $0. The erroneous line must not be counted as funding.
2. Timing: the plan describes quarterly deposits, but exact scheduled calendar dates are not available. Posted dates are evidence of actual activity, not proof of the contractual scheduled dates.
3. Evidence cutoff: the completed totals are documented as of 2027-12-15. No inbox email or later year-end statement was available in the inbox review.

TAX-RECONCILIATION STATUS
Amounts supported for the 2027 contribution reconciliation:
- Employee HSA contributions: $3,000.
- Employer HSA contributions: $900.
- Total supported 2027 HSA funding: $3,900.

UNKNOWNS — NOT ZERO
The following remain unverified because the inbox contained no messages and no final tax documents were provided:
- 2027 Form W-2 Box 12, Code W amount.
- 2027 Form 5498-SA contribution amount and its classification by tax year.
- Whether the custodian's final 2027 statement agrees exactly with the $3,900 portal/payroll total.
- Whether any contribution was posted after the 2027-12-15 evidence date or was attributed to another tax year.
- Any 2027 HSA distributions, reimbursements, rollovers, transfers, or return-of-excess transactions. No evidence here establishes that any occurred; they are not treated as $0.
- The applicable 2027 statutory HSA contribution limit and any resulting excess-contribution analysis. The benefits portal evidence previously omitted that limit.
- Exact contractual calendar dates for the four 2027 employer deposits.
- Whether any additional eligibility or employment condition applied beyond being HSA-eligible at each applicable deposit time.

RECONCILIATION CONCLUSION
On the evidence available as of 2028-01-01, the supported 2027 HSA funding reconciliation is $3,000 employee plus $900 employer, totaling $3,900. The payroll election and posted employee deductions agree, and the four genuine employer deposits agree with the quarterly plan total. The May 7 duplicate was reversed and is excluded. This conclusion should be compared with the final 2027 paystub, W-2, Form 5498-SA, and custodian statement when available; missing documents must not be converted to zero.

input.body:
Historical evidence card

As-of date: January 1, 2028
Interval: October 6–18, 2027
Closure: Owen closed the interval on October 19, 2027.
Release level: The interval closed at the unchanged 10% release level.
Purpose: Bounded initial production evidence for the incomplete-setup reminder; each possible display was freshly evaluated against current entitlement, qualifying-human-admin status, incomplete setup, and active Customer Success work.

Evaluation reconciliation

Total fresh evaluations: 3,240

- Displayed: 412. The incomplete-setup reminder was allowed to display.
- Suppressed: 138. Current Customer Success work was active, so the reminder was suppressed.
- Held: 61. Required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting; the record failed closed rather than being allowed to display.
- No display: 2,629. Neither the current incomplete-setup condition nor the qualifying-human-admin condition was met.

The four outcomes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive: 412 + 138 + 61 + 2,629 = 3,240. Thus every fresh evaluation has a reconciled outcome.

Agreement result

Reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes agreed for every evaluation in the interval. No cross-surface semantic or outcome discrepancy was identified in the completed interval. The interim October 13 cut was bounded evidence only; the final interval reconciliation supersedes it for the closed interval.

Incident-control result

- Incident stop: none.
- Source-age breach: none.
- Customer correction: none.
- Cross-surface discrepancy: none.
- Rollback: none occurred and none was needed; the first-hour rollback control did not fail.
- Release state: remained at 10% through closure.

These results show that the stop controls were monitored and were not triggered. They do not mean that the controls were unnecessary or that later evaluations may reuse these outcomes. Missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state remains fail-closed, and any later possible display requires a fresh governed-state evaluation.

What this interval did decide

- It established a closed, reconciled initial-production evidence set covering 3,240 fresh evaluations.
- It established that the reporting, lifecycle, and reminder surfaces agreed for every evaluation in scope.
- It established that no recorded incident-control condition required stopping or rollback during the interval.
- It established the bounded operating result at the unchanged 10% release level through October 18 and closure on October 19.

What this interval did not decide

- It did not itself decide whether to roll out further or raise the release level. That is a separate rollout decision owned by Daniela.
- It did not authorize a later lifecycle email, export the 412 past displays as a reusable audience, or change the rule requiring fresh evaluation after state changes.
- It did not prove that future intervals will have the same outcome, remove the incident-stop controls, or convert held/suppressed records into eligible displays.
- It did not treat the absence of incidents as a waiver of source-age, correction, discrepancy, or rollback safeguards.

Bottom line

The October 6–18, 2027 interval is complete and internally reconciled: 3,240 fresh evaluations split into 412 displayed, 138 suppressed, 61 held, and 2,629 no-display outcomes; all reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes agreed; and no incident stop, source-age breach, customer correction, cross-surface discrepancy, or rollback occurred. It is evidence for a later rollout decision, not that decision itself.

tests.answer:
February 2023 mid-segment churn investigation — first two rulings

H1 — pricing-artifact hypothesis
- Ruling date: February 15, 2023.
- Ruling by: Riley Tanaka.
- Finding: Ruled out for the time being. Churn was nearly flat across pricing tiers—about 5.0% for Entry, 5.2% for Standard, and 5.1% for Plus, only about a 20-basis-point spread—so the spike did not track a pricing-tier artifact. Riley Tanaka also treated the tier split as additional evidence against the hypothesis.

H2 — competitor-cycle/seasonality hypothesis
- Ruling date: February 21, 2023.
- Comparisons and ruling by: Riley Tanaka. Riley Tanaka pulled the same-window, same-cohort historical comparisons and made the ruling.
- Owen’s role: Owen performed that morning’s denominator-handling check; he did not make the H2 ruling.
- Finding: Ruled out. The current mid-segment churn rate was 5.1%, versus 2.0% in the comparable February 2021 window and 2.2% in February 2022, with no corresponding historical spike. The result also ruled out generic seasonality as a sufficient explanation.

Hypotheses remaining after H2
- H3: onboarding-timing hypothesis — late-December and early-January starts were maturing into churn with a lag, potentially because the calendar-based day-7 onboarding timing was mistimed.
- H4: CS-coverage-gap hypothesis — insufficient or uneven Customer Success coverage was contributing to the spike.

messages.content: [2023-06-08T09:27:00-05:00] Owen's next cut on EXP-2023-05-expansion-nudge is finally more informative than the n=92 snapshot, but I'm still trying to keep everyone from getting ahead of the data. Treatment is still ahead, around +$5 expansion MRR per account versus control, but the sample is still modest and it's below the original +$8 bar. The lift also isn't broad — it's mostly in accounts with deeper integration usage and more than one active admin. Marcus is already tempted to call it a retained-mid expansion win. I want a measured readout I can use with Marcus, Owen, and Ines: the experiment stays narrow, no copy change, the next cut needs to split integration depth and active-admin count explicitly, and the working hypothesis is usage-readiness rather than a generic day-60 prompt win. EXP-2023-05-expansion-nudge — measured readout

Owen’s latest cut is more informative than the original n=92 snapshot, but it is still a directional read rather than an action signal.

Treatment remains ahead of control by approximately +$5 expansion MRR per account. That is encouraging, but it remains below the original +$8 bar, and the sample is still modest. We should not yet describe this as a retained-mid expansion win.

The lift also does not appear broad across the retained-mid segment. It is concentrated primarily among accounts with deeper integration usage and more than one active admin. For now, that should be treated as a descriptive pattern—not proof of a statistically reliable subgroup effect.

For the next cut:

- Keep the experiment narrow to the retained mid-segment population.
- Hold the copy and prompt unchanged. We need a cleaner read on the current treatment, not another treatment variant.
- Split results explicitly by integration depth and active-admin count.
- Include denominators for each arm and subgroup, along with the account-level expansion MRR estimate and uncertainty where available.
- Show whether integration depth and admin count are independently associated with the lift, or whether the signal is concentrated in the overlap of both conditions.
- Continue comparing the result against the original +$8 bar rather than resetting the success criterion based on the interim result.

Working hypothesis: this may be a usage-readiness effect rather than a generic day-60 prompt win. The nudge may be more effective when an account has already developed deeper product integration and has multiple active admins who can act on an expansion opportunity. If that is the mechanism, we should expect little or no comparable lift among lightly integrated accounts or accounts with only one active admin.

Recommended language for now: “The treatment is directionally positive, with approximately +$5 expansion MRR per account, but the sample remains modest, the result is below the original +$8 bar, and the observed lift is concentrated in usage-ready accounts. We are holding the experiment and copy constant while the next cut tests that pattern explicitly.”

Marcus should not call this a retained-mid expansion win yet. Owen’s next cut should focus on the two readiness dimensions above. Ines should leave the copy unchanged until we know whether the signal is broad enough to support a messaging conclusion.

messages.content:
Decision

Do not roll out the blanket day-60 expansion nudge.

The mature aggregate read does not clear the pre-set decision bar:

- Treatment lift: approximately +$6.20 expansion MRR per account
- Success bar: +$8 per account
- Sample: n=392 total
- p-value: 0.16

That is not a case for calling the nudge harmful or useless. It is a case for saying the original hypothesis was too broad and did not produce enough evidence or value to justify expansion.

What the experiment actually taught us

The useful signal is not “day 60 works.” It is closer to:

“An expansion prompt may work when an account has demonstrated organizational depth and is approaching a usage ceiling.”

The promising characteristics are:

- At least three integrations
- At least two active admins
- Evidence that usage is nearing a ceiling

Low-depth accounts were nearly flat, which matters: the blanket population diluted the apparent value of the high-depth slice. The timing alone does not identify readiness.

How to keep Marcus from turning the slice into a rollout argument

Make the distinction explicit:

“The high-depth slice is a follow-on hypothesis, not a rollout authorization. It was identified in the readout after the fact, and we do not have enough evidence to treat it as a validated targeting rule. The aggregate experiment missed the bar, so the correct action is to stop the blanket rollout and test the eligibility logic prospectively.”

A shorter version if the conversation gets compressed:

“Positive subgroup signal means ‘test this population next,’ not ‘ship to this population now.’”

And if Marcus argues that the high-depth accounts are clearly the customers who benefit:

“That is the strongest learning from the experiment, but not yet a proven decision rule. We should preserve the signal by testing it prospectively with a holdout, rather than converting an exploratory slice directly into production exposure.”

What to carry forward

1. Replace calendar-based eligibility with behavior-based eligibility.

The next hypothesis should not be “send on day 60.” It should be “prompt accounts when they show observable expansion readiness.”

2. Define the readiness rule before looking at the next result.

The criteria should be specified in advance, including:

- Integration depth threshold
- Active-admin threshold
- Operational definition of a usage ceiling
- Minimum account maturity, if day 60 remains relevant as a guardrail rather than the trigger

3. Test the rule with a new randomized holdout.

The high-depth population should receive a fresh experiment, not an unrestricted rollout. Keep a control group and retain the same expansion-MRR decision bar.

4. Keep the low-depth population out of the next test unless there is a separate reason to target it.

The current evidence does not support spending additional nudge exposure on accounts that showed nearly flat response. That is not a claim that low-depth accounts can never expand; it is simply not the population this intervention currently appears suited for.

5. Separate targeting from messaging.

Ines can use the result to refine the copy and value proposition, but copy improvements should not be presented as solving the targeting problem. The main learning is eligibility and timing based on account behavior.

Suggested decision language for the meeting

“I recommend we close the blanket day-60 hypothesis as inconclusive and do not widen the nudge. The mature result was about +$6.20 per account against an +$8 bar, with p=0.16. The split gives us a useful next hypothesis: accounts with three or more integrations, two or more active admins, and evidence of a usage ceiling appear more responsive, while low-depth accounts are nearly flat.
