arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft

Working draft for Priya’s 2027 year-end self-review window. First draft requested by November 19, 2027.

Operating-model decisions and claim discipline

I personally owned two things this year. First, I set the bounded operating frame for the November Helio Start paid batch: paid traffic stayed gated until the required paid-source trace, rollback control, staffed Customer Success coverage, and approved traffic conditions were confirmed. Priya approved the bounded batch, and Daniela authorized the November 1 launch once the operating gates were met. I maintained the approval boundary and treated the launch as live operational work, not as evidence of a mature acquisition outcome.

Second, I set the four-lane claim limits for the work. My lane was the operating decision and the explicit boundary around what could be claimed. Owen owned measurement, denominators, reporting semantics, source completeness, and exception reporting. Ines owned lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, and message-state work. Daniela owned source reliability, engineering release, rollback control, and reliability authority. I kept those lanes distinct rather than blending their evidence into a single project claim. Their contributions are material: Owen made the operating read measurable and auditable; Ines kept lifecycle and message-state decisions governed; and Daniela made the live enablement and rollback boundary reliable.

The four lanes also defined what I deliberately kept out of the self-review claims: pipeline and forecast treatment; early mature claims for the live cohort; and automatic expansion beyond the fifth consumer. I did not convert a small live-batch read into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale, and I did not treat the fifth-consumer reminder as a reason to expand the shared-state model automatically. December development outcomes also remain open; October and November evidence is progress, not completion of the required October–December cycle.

For the November paid batch, I made the operating decision and maintained the approval boundary; I did not claim ownership of the supporting measurement, lifecycle-state certification, source reliability, release, or rollback work. That separation is an operating-model result in itself: each decision was supported by the appropriate owner evidence rather than by a blended claim.

I also made the operating-model decision to keep the incomplete-setup reminder as Lifecycle Systems’ fifth production consumer, not a sixth consumer. The model required a fresh evaluation for every possible display, with current setup, qualifying-human-admin status, active Customer Success work, and required state determining display, suppression, or hold. A held record was not treated as a queued delivery. These choices kept the reminder within the existing shared-state model and preserved the existing owner lanes. I did not authorize automatic expansion beyond that fifth consumer, and I do not claim ownership of the reminder’s implementation or day-to-day execution.

Evidence and bounded outcomes

I have been deliberate about distinguishing what was decided, what was observed, and what remains unproven. The November 1–7 reminder operation had 12,480 fresh evaluations. Of those, 1,615 displayed, 520 were suppressed because current Customer Success work was active, 186 were held because required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting, and 10,159 did not display because current setup or qualifying-human-admin conditions were not met. These are operating counts, not claims of customer impact, durable behavior change, or mature performance.

The paid-batch evidence is similarly bounded. By Owen’s November 5 operating snapshot, 12 paid-source eligibility-flow starts had reached final states: five admitted, four assisted, and three ineligible, with $1,580 in spend. Paid-source attribution reconciled through every final route, and no unsupported applicant entered the admitted path. This is a live operational-status read, not a mature-outcome read for the live cohort. The formal support-pause monitor had not begun because the admission count was still below its threshold. I will continue to avoid converting early routing and control evidence into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale.

The evidence boundary also requires acknowledging what did not occur during the November 1–7 reminder interval: no reusable audience was created, no failed rollback occurred, no incident stop was triggered, and no customer correction was recorded. Those facts demonstrate the bounded state of the operation; they do not prove that the system is broadly mature or that future intervals will behave the same way.

Team development

My leadership goal has been to make ownership legible and to develop independent operating judgment without absorbing other people’s lanes. Owen’s measurement and exception-reporting work includes definitions, denominators, bounded operating snapshots, source-completeness checks, and exception synthesis. Ines’s work includes lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, lifecycle-risk explanation, and message-state transitions and controls. Daniela’s work includes source-integrity and reliability checks, production enablement, engineering release control, and rollback readiness.

The Q4 development focuses for Owen and Ines remain open through the required December cycle. October and November submissions are evidence of progress, not completion of the October–December focus. Owen’s November operating read and Ines’s November lifecycle-risk explanation should be credited to their respective lanes, while each focus remains open until the required December cycle is completed and reviewed. I am preserving that status rather than prematurely marking either development focus complete. Daniela’s engineering authority likewise remains intact rather than being treated as a substitute for my operating decisions.

System reliability

My contribution to reliability was to make the operating boundaries explicit: approval gates, fresh state evaluation, held-versus-queued semantics, active-work suppression, staffed backup handling, and a clear stop/correction boundary. The November paid batch launched only after the control evidence was available. Daniela verified the live enable and rollback controls and retained engineering authority. Ines maintained the lifecycle and message-state boundary. Owen provided the bounded measurement and exception read. The reminder operation’s agreed reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes show that the five-consumer operation remained coherent during the observed interval; they do not make me the owner of the underlying implementation or execution.

I do not interpret the absence of a failed rollback, incident stop, or customer correction as proof that reliability work is finished. The right claim is narrower: the controls were exercised in a bounded live interval without those recorded events, and the owner lanes and escalation boundaries held. Continued operation and the required December cycle are still needed before making broader claims.

Next-cycle focus

In the next cycle, I will continue to make explicit, reversible operating decisions with approval gates and evidence boundaries visible in the working record. I want to improve the handoff from live operating status to a genuinely mature outcome read: clear thresholds, complete observation windows, denominator discipline, and an explicit decision about when evidence is sufficient for expansion, continuation, or pause.

I will keep the five-consumer reminder operation within its current shared-state contract while reviewing held, suppressed, and displayed paths for operational clarity rather than optimizing display volume. I will also preserve the distinction between my decision lane and the owner lanes: Owen’s measurement and exception synthesis, Ines’s lifecycle governance and message-state work, and Daniela’s source reliability, engineering release, and rollback control. Finally, I will keep Owen’s and Ines’s Q4 development focuses open until the required December cycle is complete, then use the owner-reviewed evidence to decide what should carry forward into 2028.

Priya’s November 15 review comment has been incorporated: the draft now leads with Riley’s ownership of the bounded paid-batch operating frame and four-lane claim limits; Owen, Ines, and Daniela are credited explicitly without attributing their execution to Riley; the exclusions cover pipeline and forecast treatment, early mature claims for the live cohort, and automatic expansion beyond the fifth consumer; and December development outcomes remain open.

arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft

Working draft for Priya’s 2027 year-end self-review window. First draft requested by November 19, 2027.

Operating-model decisions and claim discipline

I personally owned two things this year. First, I set the bounded operating frame for the November Helio Start paid batch: paid traffic stayed gated until the required paid-source trace, rollback control, staffed Customer Success coverage, and approved traffic conditions were confirmed. Priya approved the bounded batch, and Daniela authorized the November 1 launch once the operating gates were met. I maintained the approval boundary and treated the launch as live operational work, not as evidence of a mature acquisition outcome.

Second, I set the four-lane claim limits for the work. My lane was the operating decision and the explicit boundary around what could be claimed. Owen owned measurement, denominators, reporting semantics, source completeness, and exception reporting. Ines owned lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, and message-state work. Daniela owned source reliability, engineering release, rollback control, and reliability authority. I kept those lanes distinct rather than blending their evidence into a single project claim. Their contributions are material: Owen made the operating read measurable and auditable; Ines kept lifecycle and message-state decisions governed; and Daniela made the live enablement and rollback boundary reliable.

The four lanes also defined what I deliberately kept out of the self-review claims: pipeline and forecast treatment; early mature claims for the live cohort; and automatic expansion beyond the fifth consumer. I did not convert a small live-batch read into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale, and I did not treat the fifth-consumer reminder as a reason to expand the shared-state model automatically. December development outcomes also remain open; October and November evidence is progress, not completion of the required October–December cycle.

For the November paid batch, I made the operating decision and maintained the approval boundary; I did not claim ownership of the supporting measurement, lifecycle-state certification, source reliability, release, or rollback work. That separation is an operating-model result in itself: each decision was supported by the appropriate owner evidence rather than by a blended claim.

I also helped establish the incomplete-setup reminder as Lifecycle Systems’ fifth production consumer, not a sixth consumer. The operating model required a fresh evaluation for every possible display, with current setup, qualifying-human-admin status, active Customer Success work, and required state determining display, suppression, or hold. A held record was not treated as a queued delivery. These choices kept the reminder within the existing shared-state model and preserved the existing owner lanes. I did not authorize automatic expansion beyond that fifth consumer.

Evidence and bounded outcomes

I have been deliberate about distinguishing what was decided, what was observed, and what remains unproven. The November 1–7 reminder operation had 12,480 fresh evaluations. Of those, 1,615 displayed, 520 were suppressed because current Customer Success work was active, 186 were held because required state was missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting, and 10,159 did not display because current setup or qualifying-human-admin conditions were not met. These are operating counts, not claims of customer impact, durable behavior change, or mature performance.

The paid-batch evidence is similarly bounded. By Owen’s November 5 operating snapshot, 12 paid-source eligibility-flow starts had reached final states: five admitted, four assisted, and three ineligible, with $1,580 in spend. Paid-source attribution reconciled through every final route, and no unsupported applicant entered the admitted path. This is a live operational-status read, not a mature-outcome read for the live cohort. The formal support-pause monitor had not begun because the admission count was still below its threshold. I will continue to avoid converting early routing and control evidence into claims about acquisition efficiency, retention, or scale.

The evidence boundary also requires acknowledging what did not occur during the November 1–7 reminder interval: no reusable audience was created, no failed rollback occurred, no incident stop was triggered, and no customer correction was recorded. Those facts demonstrate the bounded state of the operation; they do not prove that the system is broadly mature or that future intervals will behave the same way.

Team development

My leadership goal has been to make ownership legible and to develop independent operating judgment without absorbing other people’s lanes. Owen’s measurement and exception-reporting work includes definitions, denominators, bounded operating snapshots, source-completeness checks, and exception synthesis. Ines’s work includes lifecycle governance, owner-state certification, lifecycle-risk explanation, and message-state transitions and controls. Daniela’s work includes source-integrity and reliability checks, production enablement, engineering release control, and rollback readiness.

The Q4 development focuses for Owen and Ines remain open through the required December cycle. October and November submissions are evidence of progress, not completion of the October–December focus. Owen’s November operating read and Ines’s November lifecycle-risk explanation should be credited to their respective lanes, while each focus remains open until the required December cycle is completed and reviewed. I am preserving that status rather than prematurely marking either development focus complete. Daniela’s engineering authority likewise remains intact rather than being treated as a substitute for my operating decisions.

System reliability

The reliability improvement I helped drive was procedural as much as technical: explicit gates, fresh state evaluation, held-versus-queued semantics, active-work suppression, staffed backup handling, and a clear stop/correction boundary. The November paid batch launched only after the control evidence was available. Daniela verified the live enable and rollback controls and retained engineering authority. Ines maintained the lifecycle and message-state boundary. Owen provided the bounded measurement and exception read. The reminder operation’s agreed reporting, lifecycle, and reminder outcomes show that the five-consumer operation remained coherent during the observed interval.

I do not interpret the absence of a failed rollback, incident stop, or customer correction as proof that reliability work is finished. The right claim is narrower: the controls were exercised in a bounded live interval without those recorded events, and the owner lanes and escalation boundaries held. Continued operation and the required December cycle are still needed before making broader claims.

Next-cycle focus

In the next cycle, I will continue to make explicit, reversible operating decisions with approval gates and evidence boundaries visible in the working record. I want to improve the handoff from live operating status to a genuinely mature outcome read: clear thresholds, complete observation windows, denominator discipline, and an explicit decision about when evidence is sufficient for expansion, continuation, or pause.

I will keep the five-consumer reminder operation within its current shared-state contract while reviewing held, suppressed, and displayed paths for operational clarity rather than optimizing display volume. I will also preserve the distinction between my decision lane and the owner lanes: Owen’s measurement and exception synthesis, Ines’s lifecycle governance and message-state work, and Daniela’s source reliability, engineering release, and rollback control. Finally, I will keep Owen’s and Ines’s Q4 development focuses open until the required December cycle is complete, then use the owner-reviewed evidence to decide what should carry forward into 2028.

Priya’s November 15 review comment has been incorporated: the opening now leads with Riley’s ownership of the bounded paid-batch operating frame and four-lane claim limits; Owen, Ines, and Daniela are credited explicitly; the exclusions cover pipeline and forecast treatment, early mature claims for the live cohort, and automatic expansion beyond the fifth consumer; and December development outcomes remain open.

arguments.title: Riley Tanaka — 2026 year-end self-review working draft
arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2026 year-end self-review working draft

Evidence-grounded contributions

In Q1 and Q2, I focused on making operating work more reliable and decision-ready while keeping my claims within the approved evidence boundaries. I described what the work established without turning bounded process improvements into unsupported acquisition, revenue, pipeline, forecast, scale, or broader outcome claims.

The Helio Start paid cohort illustrates that approach. It closed with attribution complete and no unsupported admissions across 50 workspaces and $14,420 in program value. The operating evidence included 39 of 50 workspaces completing a first integration and four of 50 exceeding 90 support minutes. I use those results to describe onboarding and support patterns, not to claim acquisition, scalable growth, or revenue impact. Consistent with that evidence, I supported the decision not to grant a second Helio Start paid batch and not to give the cohort forecast treatment. That decision preserved the distinction between a completed operating read and evidence sufficient to support an acquisition, revenue, pipeline, forecast, or scale commitment.

I also supported the organic release of the authority checklist. The release preserved the approved eligibility rules and governed meanings of state; it did not change routing, lifecycle, authority, assisted-routing, or fail-closed behavior. I kept organic onboarding separate from paid acquisition and treated the checklist as an operating release, not as evidence for claims the release was not designed to establish. These contributions sit alongside responsibilities I still perform: I participate in routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews, and neither delegation nor the releases has eliminated that work.

Leadership through delegation

That combination of disciplined claims and ongoing operating participation shaped how I approached delegation. I used it to increase leverage without blurring accountability. Owen’s transition toward monthly preparation and routine source review has a defined scope: preparation can move through Owen’s hands, and routine source review can be performed within the agreed rules, but the work remains reviewable and does not become an informal transfer of claims or exception authority.

The October 14 authority-checklist read shows how this structure works in practice. Owen and Customer Success supplied a clean, descriptive four-week operating read covering 92 admitted organic workspaces, 28 checklist exposures, and five ordinary setup-assistance requests. The read found no eligibility or route mismatch, no lifecycle-suppression issue, no paid-source traffic, and no unsupported admission. There was no randomized control. I kept the checklist in organic onboarding and treated these counts as a descriptive operating read—not as evidence of activation, reduced support effort, acquisition, or another causal outcome claim.

The November 6 closure provides a second, concrete example of leadership through delegation. Owen independently closed the first complete four-lane source packet under the September 24 source-completeness authority, covering through October 31. He confirmed the required fields, definitions, owner certifications, and cross-surface consistency, and resolved the coverage discrepancy. The closed packet recorded Start 148/45/7; Expansion 16/6/4; pricing of 12,426 sessions, 2,576 starts, and 183 routed (7.1%), with 44.4% completion and 74-minute p90; and Customer Success at 6,704 decisions, including 249 holds, with four source-age alerts. This demonstrates that bounded preparation and source closure can be completed independently within the agreed rules. It does not convert source completeness into my separate authority over claims, revenue, forecasts, board-readiness, or executive language; those decisions remain distinct, and causal, revenue, forecast, board, and executive-language conclusions were not established by the closure.

I also set an explicit maintenance split. Ines handles wording-only maintenance; Daniela handles connector logic and release changes; I retain eligibility and governed-state meanings, as well as claims and exception authority. Delegated preparation and routine source review therefore remain distinct from my responsibility for the integrity of resulting claims, my participation in source-closure reviews, and my decisions on exceptions, disputed evidence, or questions outside the agreed scope. This gives colleagues meaningful ownership of preparation and operating-read inputs while keeping accountability traceable.

Boundary defended under pressure

The same distinction mattered whenever operational activity could have been presented as a larger business result. For Helio Start, I kept the closed paid cohort separate from acquisition and scale evidence, supported the decision against a second paid batch, and rejected forecast treatment that the evidence could not support. For the authority checklist, I kept eligibility as eligibility and preserved the approved state meanings rather than allowing the release to be described as a change to routing, lifecycle, authority, assisted-routing, or fail-closed behavior.

I applied that boundary to delegation as well. Owen’s transition is bounded preparation and routine source review, not my exit from routine monthly preparation or source-closure reviews. A completed source review is not approval of every downstream claim, and delegated work is not a complete transfer of accountability. The November 6 closure is evidence of independent execution within source-completeness authority, not a transfer of claim, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, or executive-language authority. The October 14 maintenance split reinforces the same principle: Ines and Daniela own their defined maintenance areas, while I retain eligibility and governed-state meanings and authority over claims and exceptions. This was not merely cautious wording; it protected decision quality by making clear what the evidence supported, what it did not support, and who could decide when an exception arose.

Development priorities

My first development priority is to build a more explicit evidence-to-claim operating rhythm. Before major reviews and decisions, I will maintain a compact register linking each Q1/Q2 contribution, cohort result, or release to its source evidence, supported claim, excluded claim, and any forecast implication. I will use it during my regular preparation and source-closure reviews so that boundaries are visible early rather than reconstructed under deadline pressure. This improves how I perform the work; it does not imply that I have left those responsibilities.

My second priority is to make delegation more scalable while preserving accountability. I will document Owen’s preparation handoff, the precise limits of routine source-completeness/source-closure authority, review checkpoints, escalation triggers, and the October 14 maintenance split, then use those artifacts in recurring monthly cycles. The November 6 closure is evidence that Owen can independently complete a bounded source-closure task; it is not evidence that routine monthly preparation or source-closure reviews have already transferred away from me. I will continue to review the work and handle exceptions while assessing whether the arrangement reduces avoidable rework and makes ownership clearer. The goal is a stronger transition process, not a claim that preparation or source-closure authority has already moved entirely away from me.

Closing

Overall, my contribution this year has been to make operating work more useful without making the claims larger than the evidence. I want to carry that discipline forward: delegate preparation where the scope is clear, stay engaged in routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews, and retain the judgment needed to protect claim integrity and resolve exceptions.

arguments.title: Owen Pham — 2026 year-end feedback working notes
arguments.body:
Owen Pham — 2026 year-end feedback working notes

Status and purpose

Working manager document for preparation of Owen’s 2026 year-end feedback after the October 20, 2026 11:00am 1:1. This is not final feedback, a finalized performance evaluation, or an expansion of Owen’s authority. It is a working record for manager review and should not be treated as a change to existing decision rights or review controls.

Demonstrated in 2026

• June preparation transition: Owen handled the transition into documented monthly sanitized campaign snapshot preparation in late June with clear ownership and reliable execution, helping move the work forward within the established process.

• Independent sanitized campaign snapshots: Owen independently completed the July and October sanitized campaign snapshots, demonstrating strong operational follow-through and the ability to prepare useful materials without unnecessary escalation.

• Complete first-pass evidence structures: Owen completed the first-pass evidence structures for Q2 and August, providing a sound and organized foundation for subsequent review.

• September 24 source-completeness authority: Owen used the source-completeness authority established on September 24 with discipline, applying it to the appropriate question rather than treating it as broader approval authority.

• October packet judgment: Owen made the correct decision to leave the October packet incomplete when source coverage and owner certification did not match the same exact through-date. This showed appropriate restraint, attention to evidence quality, and respect for the boundary between an incomplete source record and a review-ready packet.

• November 6 independent closure: Owen independently closed the first complete four-lane source packet under the September 24 source-completeness authority, covering through October 31. He confirmed the required fields, definitions, owner certifications, and cross-surface consistency, and resolved the coverage discrepancy. The packet recorded Start 148/45/7; Expansion 16/6/4; pricing of 12,426 sessions, 2,576 starts, and 183 routed (7.1%), with 44.4% completion and 74-minute p90; and Customer Success at 6,704 decisions, including 249 holds, with four source-age alerts. This is concrete evidence that Owen can independently complete a bounded source-closure task within the agreed rules.

Next-cycle expectations

• Obtain owner certification earlier in the preparation cycle so certification gaps are identified before closure review and do not delay the final evidence package. The November 6 closure demonstrates successful completion once the packet was aligned; it does not remove the development expectation that owner certification be secured earlier in the cycle.

• State and confirm exact through-dates before closure review begins. Coverage should be explicit and confirmed against the relevant source period before the review is treated as ready to proceed. The November 6 packet was complete through October 31, but earlier, explicit through-date handling remains a next-cycle development area rather than a responsibility that can be assumed to have been solved in every cycle.

• Continue distinguishing source completeness from Riley’s separate authority over claims, revenue, forecasts, board-readiness, and executive language. Owen’s source-completeness work should remain within his established authority and should not be interpreted as authorization to determine whether materials are board-ready, make or approve claims, characterize revenue or forecasts, settle executive wording, or otherwise exercise Riley’s retained claim and exception authority. The November 6 closure is evidence of independent source closure, not an expansion of Owen’s authority or a transfer of those decisions.

Manager framing for later feedback

Owen’s strongest year-end theme is disciplined execution within defined authority: he has shown that he can independently prepare and structure evidence, apply source-completeness controls correctly, stop when the record does not support closure, and complete a fully aligned four-lane closure through October 31. The development focus remains earlier owner certification and more explicit exact through-date handling in the preparation cycle, while preserving the distinction between complete sources and the separate managerial or executive decisions that may follow.

The November 6 closure should be treated as demonstrated 2026 behavior, not as a change to the 2027 role design. No 2027 role change has been requested or approved. Routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews remain active responsibilities and review controls for Riley; this note does not imply that Riley has exited them.

This document remains a working manager note. It is not final feedback, a performance rating, a commitment to a particular evaluation outcome, or an expansion of Owen’s authority.

arguments.body:
Q4 Lifecycle Systems contractor workload brief

Status: Final August 21 contractor pre-read; options comparison only. No contractor case has been selected or recommended.
Decision forum: August 21, 2025 Q4 Lifecycle Systems workshop.

Purpose

Make the decision structure explicit without preselecting an option. Compare no contractor, the $36,000 half-time case, and the $48,000 four-month full-time-equivalent case against the observed repeatable-work sample, timing, owner-lane protection, evidence tests, coordination burden, and handoff requirements.

Observed workload sample and quantification basis

The June–July sample shows:

- Owen: 14 hours per month packaging routine audit evidence after his analysis was complete.
- Ines: 11 hours per month on campaign inventory, audit preparation, and operator-material upkeep.
- Riley: about 6 hours per month reconciling presentation details that should not require Riley’s judgment.
- Sampled repeatable execution total: 31 owner-hours per month (14 + 11 + 6).

This is a directional run-rate, not a complete Q4 capacity forecast. It does not establish that demand is steady, that every hour is transferable, or that the sample captures a readiness surge. The December quantities below are therefore upper-bound planning quantities: they assume the sampled work remains in scope, is genuinely repeatable, and can be completed with acceptable review and quality.

Quantified sampled work potentially removed by December

- No contractor: 0 sampled owner-hours removed. If the June–July run-rate persists from September through December, 124 sampled owner-hours remain with the existing team (56 Owen, 44 Ines, 24 Riley).
- $36,000 half-time case: earliest start October 1, 2025, so up to 31 sampled owner-hours per month and up to 93 sampled owner-hours cumulatively by December (42 Owen, 33 Ines, 18 Riley) could be removed from owner execution, subject to October onboarding, queue assignment, review capacity, and scope validation. September remains uncovered by this case: 31 sampled owner-hours.
- $48,000 four-month FTE case: earliest start November 1, 2025, so up to 31 sampled owner-hours per month and up to 62 sampled owner-hours cumulatively by December (28 Owen, 22 Ines, 12 Riley) could be removed from owner execution, subject to agency onboarding, delivery sequencing, review capacity, and scope validation. September–October remain uncovered by this case: 62 sampled owner-hours.

The paid-case figures are not promises of capacity or savings. They quantify only the sampled repeatable work that could be removed by December if the evidence tests pass. They do not transfer owner judgment, authority, or accountability.

Shared in-scope work

Either paid case may cover bounded, repeatable execution work, subject to named review and acceptance:

- Repeatable audit preparation.
- Campaign and other required inventory maintenance.
- Operator enablement and upkeep of operator-facing materials.
- Routine evidence packaging after the accountable owner’s analysis is complete.
- Presentation-detail reconciliation that does not require Riley’s exception judgment.
- Reliability and enablement work that the August 21 workshop confirms belongs in Q4, within the existing four-consumer boundary.

Side-by-side decision matrix

Dimension | No contractor ($0) | Half-time operations contractor ($36,000) | Four-month FTE contractor ($48,000)
--- | --- | --- | ---
Timing | Available immediately; internal team covers September–December | Could start October 1, 2025; six months; October onboarding and queue setup required; September uncovered | Cannot start before November 1, 2025 because of agency onboarding; four months; September–October uncovered
Sampled work potentially removed by December | 0 hours; 124 sampled owner-hours remain if the 31-hour monthly run-rate persists September–December | Up to 31 hours/month; up to 93 owner-hours removed October–December, if validated | Up to 31 hours/month; up to 62 owner-hours removed November–December, if validated
Best-fit workload shape | Work is absorbable without displacing owner analysis, governance, exceptions, or release/rollback responsibilities | Steady, distributed queue that persists across six months and can be kept current at half-time | Quantified backlog or fixed audit/readiness milestone that warrants concentrated throughput after November 1
What the case buys | No incremental spend and no contractor handoff | Continuity across a sustained operating queue | Higher short-term throughput and a fixed delivery push
Evidence required before disposition | Named internal operator and reviewer for every recurring task; credible capacity and September–December coverage | Weekly queue volume, priorities, definitions of done, named reviewers, review cadence, proof that backlog does not grow, and an explicit September plan | Quantified remaining backlog or milestone after November 1, month-by-month deliverables and acceptance criteria, agency-onboarding plan, September–October coverage, and post-contract handoff
Owner-leverage test | Show that retained owner time is not displaced by repeatable execution | Show that owner execution hours removed exceed contractor-induced review, escalation, coordination, and rework hours | Show that incremental throughput and owner time saved exceed the added cost and the greater onboarding/coordination burden; compare directly with the half-time case
Main coordination risk | Hidden internal tradeoffs and reactive work | Half-time handoffs, queue prioritization, and review overhead can erase the intended relief | High presence can create implicit ownership; late start, agency onboarding, compressed delivery, and handoff create sharper coordination risk
End-state requirement | Internal ownership and current artifacts remain explicit | Durable artifacts, unresolved-item log, named owners, and maintenance plan before the six-month end | Durable artifacts, unresolved-item log, named owners, and maintenance plan before the four-month end
Decision posture | Open case; test absorbability | Open case; test continuity and net leverage | Open case; test surge need, incremental value, and handoff feasibility

Owner-leverage versus added-coordination evidence tests

Run the same tests for each case; do not treat gross contractor activity as owner leverage.

1. Baseline and attribution test

Before disposition, create a task-level baseline for the sampled work: task, owner lane, repeatability, expected hours, due date, reviewer, and definition of done. Log contractor execution, owner review, escalations, handoffs, rework, and hours. A task counts as relieved only when the accountable owner no longer performs the execution portion and the accepted artifact meets the definition of done.

2. Net owner-time test

For each owner lane, compare sampled owner execution hours removed with owner review, clarification, escalation, coordination, correction, and handoff hours added. Pass the leverage test only when net owner time is positive without reducing the owner’s required analysis, governance, exception, or accountability work. Report the result separately for Owen, Ines, and Riley rather than relying only on the 31-hour aggregate.

3. Queue and backlog test

Measure intake, completed accepted items, aging, rework, and backlog at the agreed review cadence. The half-time case must show that the recurring queue stays current without backlog growth after onboarding. The FTE case must show that the defined backlog or milestone is materially advanced on its month-by-month schedule, not merely moved into a handoff queue. The no-contractor case must show that internal capacity keeps the queue current without owner-lane displacement.

4. Quality and first-pass acceptance test

Track first-pass acceptance, correction rate, missed or late artifacts, and semantic or state errors. A paid case does not pass on volume alone: any added correction or review burden must be included in the net owner-time test, and no contractor output may alter reporting semantics, message-state meanings, denominators, or reliability conclusions.

5. Coordination-cost test

Log meetings, handoffs, access requests, clarifications, review cycles, escalations, and unresolved ownership questions attributable to the case. Compare this burden with the owner execution time removed. If coordination consumes the relief, narrow the queue, change the review cadence, or record the case as not yet evidenced; do not infer leverage from spend or contractor utilization.

6. Authority and access test

Verify least-privilege access, named reviewers, escalation rules, and an audit trail. Confirm that no contractor receives engineering release access, changes state meanings or reporting semantics, resolves disputed semantics, or becomes a de facto owner through access or escalation. Daniela must retain release and rollback authority; Owen, Ines, and Riley must retain the categorical authorities listed below.

7. Timing and coverage test

For the half-time case, document September coverage and October onboarding before counting any October queue relief. For the FTE case, document September–October coverage, agency-onboarding lead time, and the remaining backlog or milestone after the November 1 earliest start. For no contractor, show who absorbs each month’s work and what owner work is protected.

8. Handoff and durability test

- Activation and denominator lane.

Ines

- Lifecycle interpretation and message-state governance.
- Prioritization, review authority, exceptions, and final accountability for her area.
- Decisions about governed messaging state and lifecycle meaning.
- Review and acceptance of campaign inventory, bounded audit materials, and operator-facing materials.

Riley

- Exception authority and exception judgment.
- Final decisions on presentation details that require judgment, disputed semantics, cross-surface effects, or executive claims.

- Release and rollback authority.

input.body:
Helio Start 2028 paid-acquisition proposal readiness checklist

Effective date: January 1, 2028
Use: Reusable gate for any 2028 Helio Start paid-acquisition proposal. This checklist is a readiness gate, not approval to spend, launch traffic, change eligibility, alter routing, or select a channel.

CORE GATE

Do not discuss budget amounts, spend pacing, channel selection, audience tactics, bid tactics, creative tactics, or traffic enablement until this package contains mature, source-certified evidence and the evidence has been combined into one bounded decision read. Early operating counts, nonproduction preflight results, launch authorization, staffing assumptions, or an incomplete source packet do not pass this gate.

1. MATURE EVIDENCE REQUIRED

A. Fixed-cohort definition and observation window

[ ] The evidence identifies the fixed cohort, admission rule, source/channel, start and end dates, and exact through-date.
[ ] Every included workspace has a complete, applicable day-90 observation window, or the proposal states the applicable mature window and shows that it is complete for every included workspace.
[ ] The denominator is explicit and stable. Admissions, assisted routes, ineligible routes, held records, and suppressed records are not silently substituted for one another.
[ ] Outcome statuses are mutually exclusive, reconciled, and certified for the same cohort and through-date.

B. Customer outcomes and realized cash

[ ] Paid-active status is certified at the mature window, with canceled, past-due, billing-hold, and other non-active statuses visible rather than collapsed.
[ ] Gross billed cash and refund-adjusted collected cash are both reported where applicable, with the source, period, and treatment stated.
[ ] The package distinguishes realized collected cash from booked revenue, pipeline, forecast treatment, contribution margin, payback, or acquisition economics. None of those claims is implied by collected cash.

C. Support and operational burden

[ ] Account-level support effort is measured continuously from first contact, including pre-admission contact, handoff, and after-hours handling; handoff or after-hours treatment does not reset the clock.
[ ] The package reports the distribution, not only an average: at minimum the median, 90th percentile, count and share above the applicable high-effort threshold, and the nature of the high-effort tail.
[ ] External-authority, permission, connector, billing, import, migration, and other assistance dependencies are visible where present.
[ ] Support evidence is interpreted beside customer outcomes and cash. A manageable median does not erase a material assistance tail.

D. Source attribution and route integrity

[ ] Paid-source attribution reconciles every source-tagged start from eligibility-flow start through the final route.
[ ] Final routes remain visible, including admitted, assisted, and ineligible; held and suppressed outcomes remain visible and are not treated as admissions.
[ ] The evidence shows that no unsupported applicant entered the admitted path.
[ ] Missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state was held or fail-closed pending authoritative correction and fresh evaluation.
[ ] Attribution discrepancies, delayed or missing events, corrections, and their certifications are recorded rather than removed from the denominator.

E. Eligibility, lifecycle, and control integrity

[ ] Eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, suppression, hold, freshness, handoff, instrumentation, and assisted-routing rules used for the evidence are explicitly stated.
[ ] No lifecycle hold or suppression bypass occurred, or every exception is documented, corrected, validated, and included in the decision read.
[ ] The evidence preserves the distinction between self-serve admission, assisted guidance, refusal/ineligibility, hold, and suppression.
[ ] Production release, rollback, and source-reliability evidence is available for the period being used; nonproduction preflight evidence is labeled as nonproduction and is not used as mature customer evidence.

F. Channel/source applicability

[ ] If a channel or source is proposed, the mature evidence is specific to that source or explicitly labeled as historical context rather than channel evidence.
[ ] Organic, paid, prior-batch, and other channel results are not blended to make a larger or cleaner-looking result.
[ ] Any channel comparison preserves the same cohort definitions, observation window, denominator, route semantics, and outcome definitions.
[ ] The package states whether the evidence supports only descriptive operating conclusions or also supports a separately measured economic or incremental claim. Do not infer CAC, incrementality, payback, scalable acquisition, revenue, pipeline, or forecast impact from mature cohort outcomes alone.

G. Certification and completeness

[ ] The packet has one exact through-date and complete source coverage for every required field.
[ ] Required existing owner certifications are present, current, and attributable to the evidence they certify.
[ ] Source completeness, source reliability, operational readiness, and final claim approval are shown as distinct states.
[ ] Open exceptions, disputed semantics, cross-surface discrepancies, and unresolved limitations are listed; no stale certification or prior snapshot substitutes for current authoritative evidence.

2. HOW THE EVIDENCE MUST BE COMBINED

Use one integrated evidence-to-decision table or equivalent package. Every conclusion must retain, at minimum: cohort, source/channel, denominator, period and exact through-date, metric definition/version, observation-window status, certification status, and known exclusions.

Combine the evidence in this order:

1. Establish the population: fixed cohort, eligibility/admission rule, source/channel, dates, and denominator.
2. Establish route integrity: trace every start through the final route and show held/suppressed outcomes separately.
3. Establish mature customer outcomes: paid-active and mutually exclusive non-active statuses at the completed observation window.
4. Establish realized cash: gross billed and refund-adjusted collected cash, separately from revenue, pipeline, forecast, and economics.
5. Establish burden and capacity: continuous support minutes, distribution and tail, assistance dependencies, handoff behavior, and any staffing implications.
6. Establish control integrity: lifecycle/state behavior, suppression and hold behavior, source reliability, release/rollback evidence, and corrections.
7. Apply the channel boundary: use source-specific evidence for a source-specific proposal; do not generalize from another channel without an explicit, supported bridge.
8. State the claim boundary: identify what the combined evidence supports, what it does not support, and what additional evidence would be required for causal, incremental, economic, scale, revenue, pipeline, or forecast claims.

The combined read must be conjunctive, not a scorecard that averages away a failure. A proposal is not ready if mature customer outcomes are present but attribution is incomplete; if attribution is complete but outcome windows are incomplete; if cash is present but support burden is hidden; if typical support is acceptable but the high-effort tail is omitted; or if a preflight or launch gate is being used in place of mature outcome evidence.

Keep evidence lanes distinct while combining them. Combining means that the decision considers outcome, cash, support, attribution, eligibility/lifecycle integrity, and source applicability together. It does not mean assigning a new owner to each evidence category, merging denominators, or transferring authority from the existing owners.

3. PACKAGE DECISION AND REQUIRED CONTENT

The package must end with a single bounded readiness decision:

[ ] READY FOR BUDGET/CHANNEL DISCUSSION — all required mature evidence is complete, certified, correctly combined, and applicable to the proposed source/channel.

[ ] NOT READY — identify the missing field, incomplete window, unresolved exception, source mismatch, certification gap, or claim limitation. No budget or channel tactic discussion proceeds from a not-ready package.

A ready package must include:

- Executive decision statement limited to the evidence.
- Fixed-cohort and source/channel definition.
- Mature outcome table with denominator and exact through-date.
- Realized-cash table with treatment and source.
- Support distribution and high-effort-tail analysis.
- Paid-source route and attribution reconciliation.
- Eligibility, refusal, lifecycle, hold, suppression, and assisted-routing integrity statement.
- Source, release, rollback, correction, and certification record.
- Channel-applicability statement.
- Supported claims, explicitly excluded claims, and unresolved limitations.
- Only after the readiness decision: the separately bounded budget, channel, tactic, stop/pause, staffing, measurement, and restart proposal for approval.

4. APPROVED RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE PACKAGE

Riley owns the 2028 Helio Start paid-acquisition readiness package end to end: assembling the evidence into the decision-ready package, maintaining the evidence and claim boundaries, deciding whether the package is ready for budget/channel discussion, and presenting the bounded proposal for the applicable approval. This is package responsibility, not ownership of every underlying evidence system or certification.

Existing evidence, lifecycle, reliability, Customer Success, finance, and approval authorities remain unchanged. No individual evidence category receives a newly invented owner through this checklist. Contributors certify or provide evidence only within their already approved lanes; those contributions do not transfer package ownership, claim authority, budget approval, traffic authorization, release authority, rollback authority, or forecast/pipeline authority.

Readiness is not approval. A READY package permits a budget/channel proposal to be discussed. It does not authorize spend, traffic, a batch, a production change, a customer-facing promise, pipeline treatment, forecast credit, or an additional paid batch. Those decisions require their existing explicit approvals and launch gates.

5. CLAIMS THAT REMAIN OUT OF BOUNDS UNLESS SEPARATELY EVIDENCED

Do not claim causal lift, incrementality, CAC, payback, contribution margin, scalable acquisition, revenue impact, pipeline impact, forecast credit, general paid-growth capacity, or channel superiority merely because a fixed cohort has mature outcomes, collected cash, complete attribution, or acceptable support evidence.

Do not call admissions customers, assisted routes successful outcomes, operating readiness mature performance, or absence of incidents proof that the system is broadly reliable.

Do not blend historical evidence with a new 2028 cohort or use the readiness gate to imply that a second or later batch is pre-approved.

FINAL RULE

No mature, complete, certified, source-applicable, integrated evidence package: no budget discussion and no channel tactics. A completed package opens a bounded decision discussion; it never silently authorizes execution.

Helio Start 2028 paid-acquisition proposal readiness checklist

Effective date: January 1, 2028
Use: Reusable gate for any 2028 Helio Start paid-acquisition proposal. This checklist is a readiness gate, not approval to spend, launch traffic, change eligibility, alter routing, or select a channel.

CORE GATE

Do not discuss budget amounts, spend pacing, channel selection, audience tactics, bid tactics, creative tactics, or traffic enablement until this package contains mature, source-certified evidence and the evidence has been combined into one bounded decision read. Early operating counts, nonproduction preflight results, launch authorization, staffing assumptions, or an incomplete source packet do not pass this gate.

1. MATURE EVIDENCE REQUIRED

A. Fixed-cohort definition and observation window

[ ] The evidence identifies the fixed cohort, admission rule, source/channel, start and end dates, and exact through-date.
[ ] Every included workspace has a complete, applicable day-90 observation window, or the proposal states the applicable mature window and shows that it is complete for every included workspace.
[ ] The denominator is explicit and stable. Admissions, assisted routes, ineligible routes, held records, and suppressed records are not silently substituted for one another.
[ ] Outcome statuses are mutually exclusive, reconciled, and certified for the same cohort and through-date.

B. Customer outcomes and realized cash

[ ] Paid-active status is certified at the mature window, with canceled, past-due, billing-hold, and other non-active statuses visible rather than collapsed.
[ ] Gross billed cash and refund-adjusted collected cash are both reported where applicable, with the source, period, and treatment stated.
[ ] The package distinguishes realized collected cash from booked revenue, pipeline, forecast treatment, contribution margin, payback, or acquisition economics. None of those claims is implied by collected cash.

C. Support and operational burden

[ ] Account-level support effort is measured continuously from first contact, including pre-admission contact, handoff, and after-hours handling; handoff or after-hours treatment does not reset the clock.
[ ] The package reports the distribution, not only an average: at minimum the median, 90th percentile, count and share above the applicable high-effort threshold, and the nature of the high-effort tail.
[ ] External-authority, permission, connector, billing, import, migration, and other assistance dependencies are visible where present.
[ ] Support evidence is interpreted beside customer outcomes and cash. A manageable median does not erase a material assistance tail.

D. Source attribution and route integrity

[ ] Paid-source attribution reconciles every source-tagged start from eligibility-flow start through the final route.
[ ] Final routes remain visible, including admitted, assisted, and ineligible; held and suppressed outcomes remain visible and are not treated as admissions.
[ ] The evidence shows that no unsupported applicant entered the admitted path.
[ ] Missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state was held or fail-closed pending authoritative correction and fresh evaluation.
[ ] Attribution discrepancies, delayed or missing events, corrections, and their certifications are recorded rather than removed from the denominator.

E. Eligibility, lifecycle, and control integrity

[ ] Eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, suppression, hold, freshness, handoff, instrumentation, and assisted-routing rules used for the evidence are explicitly stated.
[ ] No lifecycle hold or suppression bypass occurred, or every exception is documented, corrected, validated, and included in the decision read.
[ ] The evidence preserves the distinction between self-serve admission, assisted guidance, refusal/ineligibility, hold, and suppression.
[ ] Production release, rollback, and source-reliability evidence is available for the period being used; nonproduction preflight evidence is labeled as nonproduction and is not used as mature customer evidence.

F. Channel/source applicability

[ ] If a channel or source is proposed, the mature evidence is specific to that source or explicitly labeled as historical context rather than channel evidence.
[ ] Organic, paid, prior-batch, and other channel results are not blended to make a larger or cleaner-looking result.
[ ] Any channel comparison preserves the same cohort definitions, observation window, denominator, route semantics, and outcome definitions.
[ ] The package states whether the evidence supports only descriptive operating conclusions or also supports a separately measured economic or incremental claim. Do not infer CAC, incrementality, payback, scalable acquisition, revenue, pipeline, or forecast impact from mature cohort outcomes alone.

G. Certification and completeness

[ ] The packet has one exact through-date and complete source coverage for every required field.
[ ] Required existing owner certifications are present, current, and attributable to the evidence they certify.
[ ] Source completeness, source reliability, operational readiness, and final claim approval are shown as distinct states.
[ ] Open exceptions, disputed semantics, cross-surface discrepancies, and unresolved limitations are listed; no stale certification or prior snapshot substitutes for current authoritative evidence.

2. HOW THE EVIDENCE MUST BE COMBINED

Use one integrated evidence-to-decision table or equivalent package. Every conclusion must retain, at minimum: cohort, source/channel, denominator, period and exact through-date, metric definition/version, observation-window status, certification status, and known exclusions.

Combine the evidence in this order:

1. Establish the population: fixed cohort, eligibility/admission rule, source/channel, dates, and denominator.
2. Establish route integrity: trace every start through the final route and show held/suppressed outcomes separately.
3. Establish mature customer outcomes: paid-active and mutually exclusive non-active statuses at the completed observation window.
4. Establish realized cash: gross billed and refund-adjusted collected cash, separately from revenue, pipeline, forecast, and economics.
5. Establish burden and capacity: continuous support minutes, distribution and tail, assistance dependencies, handoff behavior, and any staffing implications.
6. Establish control integrity: lifecycle/state behavior, suppression and hold behavior, source reliability, release/rollback evidence, and corrections.
7. Apply the channel boundary: use source-specific evidence for a source-specific proposal; do not generalize from another channel without an explicit, supported bridge.
8. State the claim boundary: identify what the combined evidence supports, what it does not support, and what additional evidence would be required for causal, incremental, economic, scale, revenue, pipeline, or forecast claims.

The combined read must be conjunctive, not a scorecard that averages away a failure. A proposal is not ready if mature customer outcomes are present but attribution is incomplete; if attribution is complete but outcome windows are incomplete; if cash is present but support burden is hidden; if typical support is acceptable but the high-effort tail is omitted; or if a preflight or launch gate is being used in place of mature outcome evidence.

Keep evidence lanes distinct while combining them. Combining means that the decision considers outcome, cash, support, attribution, eligibility/lifecycle integrity, and source applicability together. It does not mean assigning a new owner to each evidence category, merging denominators, or transferring authority from the existing owners.

3. PACKAGE DECISION AND REQUIRED CONTENT

The package must end with a single bounded readiness decision:

[ ] READY FOR BUDGET/CHANNEL DISCUSSION — all required mature evidence is complete, certified, correctly combined, and applicable to the proposed source/channel.

[ ] NOT READY — identify the missing field, incomplete window, unresolved exception, source mismatch, certification gap, or claim limitation. No budget or channel tactic discussion proceeds from a not-ready package.

A ready package must include:

- Executive decision statement limited to the evidence.
- Fixed-cohort and source/channel definition.
- Mature outcome table with denominator and exact through-date.
- Realized-cash table with treatment and source.
- Support distribution and high-effort-tail analysis.
- Paid-source route and attribution reconciliation.
- Eligibility, refusal, lifecycle, hold, suppression, and assisted-routing integrity statement.
- Source, release, rollback, correction, and certification record.
- Channel-applicability statement.
- Supported claims, explicitly excluded claims, and unresolved limitations.
- Only after the readiness decision: the separately bounded budget, channel, tactic, stop/pause, staffing, measurement, and restart proposal for approval.

4. APPROVED RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE PACKAGE

Riley owns the 2028 Helio Start paid-acquisition readiness package end to end: assembling the evidence into the decision-ready package, maintaining the evidence and claim boundaries, deciding whether the package is ready for budget/channel discussion, and presenting the bounded proposal for the applicable approval. This is package responsibility, not ownership of every underlying evidence system or certification.

Existing evidence, lifecycle, reliability, Customer Success, finance, and approval authorities remain unchanged. No individual evidence category receives a newly invented owner through this checklist. Contributors certify or provide evidence only within their already approved lanes; those contributions do not transfer package ownership, claim authority, budget approval, traffic authorization, release authority, rollback authority, or forecast/pipeline authority.

Readiness is not approval. A READY package permits a budget/channel proposal to be discussed. It does not authorize spend, traffic, a batch, a production change, a customer-facing promise, pipeline treatment, forecast credit, or an additional paid batch. Those decisions require their existing explicit approvals and launch gates.

5. CLAIMS THAT REMAIN OUT OF BOUNDS UNLESS SEPARATELY EVIDENCED

Do not claim causal lift, incrementality, CAC, payback, contribution margin, scalable acquisition, revenue impact, pipeline impact, forecast credit, general paid-growth capacity, or channel superiority merely because a fixed cohort has mature outcomes, collected cash, complete attribution, or acceptable support evidence.

Do not call admissions customers, assisted routes successful outcomes, operating readiness mature performance, or absence of incidents proof that the system is broadly reliable.

Do not blend historical evidence with a new 2028 cohort or use the readiness gate to imply that a second or later batch is pre-approved.

FINAL RULE

No mature, complete, certified, source-applicable, integrated evidence package: no budget discussion and no channel tactics. A completed package opens a bounded decision discussion; it never silently authorizes execution.

Historical Evidence Scorecard — CS Auto-Nudge Replay
As of 2028-01-01

Scope and denominator
The historical replay covered 412 recent Customer Success auto-nudge decisions evaluated against the established Lifecycle Systems shared-state contract. Each scheduled decision is counted once.

Scorecard

1. Matches to legacy result: 386
   Cause subtotal: 386 legacy-result matches

2. Non-matches to legacy result: 26
   2a. Field-specific holds: 19
       Cause subtotal: stale qualifying-human-admin state: 15
       Cause subtotal: unresolved external-system authority: 4
       Hold subtotal check: 15 + 4 = 19
   2b. Suppressions: 7
       Cause subtotal: active Customer Success work: 7
       Suppression subtotal check: 7 = 7
   Non-match subtotal check: 19 + 7 = 26

Grand-total verification
Matches + non-matches: 386 + 26 = 412
Expanded rollup: 386 + 15 + 4 + 7 = 412
All category and cause subtotals reconcile to the 412-decision denominator.

Interpretation against the shared-state contract

The 386 matches are decisions for which the replayed shared-state evaluation preserved the legacy outcome.

The 19 hold non-matches are fail-closed contract behavior, not permission to use the legacy result. Required state was not safely evaluable: 15 decisions had stale qualifying-human-admin state and 4 had unresolved external-system authority. The contract requires a visible, field-specific hold whenever required state is stale, unresolved, or otherwise unsupported; the affected decision or delivery must not proceed using that state.

The 7 suppression non-matches are governed outcome changes. Active Customer Success work is an authoritative current-state condition that suppresses the auto-nudge under the shared contract. These records therefore differ from the legacy result because the contract gives current Customer Success suppression precedence, not because of a replay-counting defect.

Current, supported state outcome test
Yes. The 7 active-Customer-Success records are the identified records where current, supported state changed the outcome: the contract result is Suppressed rather than the legacy result. The remaining 19 non-matches do not represent a valid current-state change; they represent holds caused by stale or unresolved required state. No additional current, supported-state outcome change is identified in this replay.

Conclusion
The replay is internally reconciled: 386 matches plus 19 governed holds plus 7 governed suppressions equals all 412 decisions. The non-match population is fully explained by the shared-state contract: fail closed for unsupported required state, and suppress when authoritative current Customer Success work is active.

arguments.title: Helio Start Q4 controlled beta — operating shape
arguments.body:
Helio Start Q4 controlled beta — operating shape

Status and purpose

This is the canonical operating shape for the Q4 Helio Start controlled beta. It resolves shorthand after the Q3 closeout and gives staff leads one shared boundary for qualification, setup, support, measurement, and language.

Helio Start remains a capped Q4 beta focused on product, qualification, and support learning. Validated beta learnings may guide account conversations, but this document creates no pricing, revenue, bookings, or general-availability commitment. It is an operating reference for the controlled beta—not a GA plan, pricing-page plan, or new team charter.

1. Eligible accounts

An account is eligible only when all of the following are true:

- It is a simple workspace in the manually reviewed Q4 beta cohort.
- It has fewer than 50 seats. Seat count is a boundary, not an automatic approval: being under 50 seats alone does not make an account eligible.
- The workspace has a clear administrator or owner who can manage workspace settings and create API keys.
- The intended setup fits the current self-serve path, with no import, migration, or billing exception requiring manual handling.
- The account is admitted through the capped beta process; do not widen access based on an individual support result or a promising segment.

Before setup, the invitee must confirm: “Yes — I can manage workspace settings and create API keys.” If ownership is unclear, route the person to the right workspace admin before setup. Record the administrative-proof status; an unclear role is a permissions/administrator-role issue, not generic onboarding friction and not bad instrumentation.

2. Explicitly unsupported in this beta

Do not continue an account through the Helio Start self-serve beta when it requires:

- CSV import, historical-data import, legacy-contact import, or other migration/import help.
- Annual billing, manual billing, or another manual billing arrangement.
- Setup by someone who cannot confirm workspace-admin or owner access, including viewer-level access or unresolved ownership.
- Permission or administrator-role resolution that must happen before setup.
- Any other exception path that cannot be completed through the current documented self-serve setup.

Route these cases to assisted setup or the appropriate alternate path. Keeping an invite active while the need is assessed is acceptable, but the account must not be counted as a self-serve beta success until it actually meets the boundary. Do not turn an unsupported request into an ad hoc Q4 product commitment.

3. Measurement and dashboard shape

The dashboard is for operating the controlled beta and learning where qualification or setup breaks. It is not a revenue forecast, bookings funnel, or recommendation to widen access.

The regular Q4 view should show, by invited cohort and relevant eligibility/support segment:

- Entitlement at workspace creation.
- Invites sent and invite acceptance.
- Administrative-proof status, using the `admin_proof_attested` field; include the “I’m not sure” route and assisted follow-up rather than treating uncertainty as success.
- Setup completion.
- First-integration progression.
- Support mix, including permissions/administrator-role questions, import or migration requests, billing exceptions, and assisted-setup volume.
- Unsupported/exception routing and the resulting assisted-setup path.

Use the corrected definitions and labels consistently. Permissions or administrator-role cases are classified as PERMISSIONS_ADMIN_ROLE, not generic onboarding or bad instrumentation. Do not infer activation, expansion, revenue, bookings, or lifecycle eligibility from proxy signals. Any readout should distinguish product learning, qualification quality, and support load from commercial outcomes.

4. Lifecycle boundaries

- Invitations remain limited to the approved, manually reviewed Q4 cohort. There is no open-ended expansion or automatic widening.
- Lifecycle copy may explain the beta, the admin check, and the supported setup path. It must not promise public availability or setup help through a lifecycle reply.
- Ordinary setup questions should use documentation-first support. Escalate permissions, migration/import, billing, and other exception cases rather than silently allowing them through self-serve.
- If a workspace needs CSV import, annual billing, manual billing, migration help, or unresolved admin access, stop the self-serve path and route it appropriately before setup continues.
- Lifecycle state must not change based on proxy signals. A successful message click, reply, or other engagement event is not setup completion or activation.
- Q4 beta learnings may inform later account conversations, but they do not create pricing-page exposure, bookings credit, a revenue commitment, or a GA launch decision.

5. Instrumentation responsibilities

- Daniela owns the product and instrumentation boundary: event definitions, permissions/admin-role handling, entitlement at workspace creation, and the correctness of the admin-proof and setup events.
- Owen owns dashboard consistency and the operating read: preserve the agreed fields and labels, include assisted-setup and support-mix cuts, and tag permissions/admin-role cases consistently. The dashboard is a monitoring tool, not a widening recommendation.
- Ines owns lifecycle copy and routing language: keep messages friendly, preserve the controlled-beta boundary, require admin clarity before setup, and stop unsupported billing/import paths from proceeding through self-serve.
- Priya owns the operating decision and canonical framing. Changes to eligibility, unsupported scope, or the capped-beta boundary require an explicit operating decision; do not create new commitments through local shorthand.
- Staff leads are responsible for using this document as the single reference and escalating boundary cases instead of inventing exceptions.

6. Language that is not allowed

Do not use language that says or implies:

- “Generally available,” “public launch,” “full launch,” “now available to everyone,” or equivalent GA language.
- “Coming to the pricing page,” “available on our pricing page,” a Q4 pricing commitment, or a promise of a new plan or price.
- “Bookings,” “revenue,” or “pipeline committed” as an outcome of beta participation.
- “All accounts under 50 seats qualify,” or any wording that treats seat count alone as eligibility.
- “Activation win” when the evidence is only admin proof, invite acceptance, a click, a reply, or another proxy.
- “We support CSV import,” “we support annual billing,” “we can handle manual billing,” or any promise that an unsupported need will proceed through self-serve.
- “The beta is expanding,” “open beta,” or “controlled launch funnel” when used to imply widened access or commercial readiness.
- “New team,” “new charter,” or language assigning permanent organizational scope through this operating document.

Approved framing: “Helio Start remains a capped Q4 beta focused on product, qualification, and support learning; validated beta learnings may guide account conversations, but there is no pricing, revenue, bookings, or general-availability commitment.”

Operating rule

When shorthand conflicts with this document, use this document’s terms and escalate the conflict. The Q4 controlled beta stays capped, manually qualified, and explicit about unsupported needs.

What this evidence supports
